item.title: San Antonio Fights Plan to Turn Warehouse Into ICE Detention Center
item.description:
With roughly seven weeks until a Democratic majority takes over Congress, San Antonio is using a lawsuit to stall the Trump administration’s plan to turn a warehouse into a detention center for 1,500 immigrants.

Representative Joaquin Castro, a Democrat who represents part of the city, hopes the party’s new majority in Congress can block the project for good when it takes power in January.

“We are just getting going now,” Mr. Castro said. “Those places, those warehouses, are not suited for people.”

The projects have faced resistance and legal defeats, and several have been scrapped.

In San Antonio, Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones and other officials have said they have been kept in the dark since February, when the government purchased the sprawling warehouse for $66 million.

The city sued last month to stop work there until the federal government studies its effects on its neighborhood, joining nearly a dozen other cities, states and nonprofit groups to challenge such plans in court.

“In their rush to convert warehouses into Amazon-like store-and-ship facilities for immigrants, defendants have trampled over federal law designed to protect the city and other stakeholders’ interests,” San Antonio’s lawsuit reads.

The city, like others that have sued, argues that the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has skipped legally required environmental reviews. The argument has already slowed the agency’s plans elsewhere: A federal judge in Maryland recently blocked a similar warehouse conversion on the same grounds. ICE has paused or dropped plans in at least five other states.

In San Antonio, the City Attorney’s Office said it was in talks with the Justice Department over a deal that would pause both the lawsuit and the work on the warehouse.

Ms. Jones said in a statement that she wants to cooperate with Democrats in Austin and Washington to resist ICE’s aggressive crackdown.

“I look forward to working with them on those approaches, which must include preventing the establishment of an ICE detention facility in San Antonio,” Ms. Jones said.

ICE did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

Under the Trump administration, immigration arrests have surged in San Antonio. The area, which is majority Latino, has an estimated 100,000 undocumented residents, city officials said.

At St. Margaret Mary Catholic Church, less than a 15-minute drive from the proposed detention center, fears have run rampant among the many immigrant parishioners, the Rev. Jimmy Drennan said. In the months before the midterm elections, many called him to ask for his help in locating missing loved ones, whom they presume have been taken by ICE.

The warehouse project makes the threat concrete, he said.

“They are going to fill it up with our children’s friends, colleagues, neighbors and the people who occupy our churches,” Father Drennan said.

Mayor Jones and Mr. Castro have said that the troubles at other such facilities in Texas are cautionary tales.

At the Dilley Immigration Processing Center, about 73 miles south of San Antonio, migrants have complained about the lack of healthy food and medical care, and unsanitary conditions.

Advocates filed a legal motion last month demanding better conditions at Camp East Montana, the nation’s largest immigration detention center, which is inside the Fort Bliss military base in El Paso.

A center in Laredo came under scrutiny this month after the death of a Mexican man, who relatives said was a legal U.S. resident. His daughter said he had not received medicine for a heart condition, diabetes and high blood pressure. An ICE official denied that.

Democrats taking over Congress in January intend to oversee ICE and other immigration agencies closely, using money as a primary lever. Spending bills could be written to withhold or pull back money from agencies that have already received more than $100 billion.

“ICE would be wise to pause the purchases or sales of all of those ICE warehouses,” Mr. Castro said.

The prospect of stopping the San Antonio center is not universally popular. Two council members who lean conservative, Marc Whyte and Misty Spears, disagreed with their colleagues on the question.

“Federal law controls immigration, and City Hall has no business interfering,” they said in a joint statement. “Our residents sent us here to keep them safe, fix our infrastructure and make San Antonio a better place to live. Washington sets immigration policy. We’ve got more than enough work to do right here at home.”

But resistance is growing. A march last month organized by a county commissioner, Tommy Calvert, drew hundreds.

“The facility is woefully inadequate for human beings,” Mr. Calvert said.

Father Drennan said that many of his parishioners feared that they might end up locked inside the 639,595-square-foot warehouse.

“They are trying to make San Antonio the epicenter of the immigration movement, and it’s creating a great sense of fear and anger within the people of our community,” Father Drennan said of the federal government.

item.title: How the Legacy of Torture Has Vexed the Quest for 9/11 Justice
item.description:
The Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks left the World Trade Center in ruins, thousands dead and a stunned nation fearful of what might come next.

In a series of secret actions, the administration of George W. Bush charted a new course to try to prevent more attacks. Dozens of suspected terrorists were spirited off to secret sites for years. Many were tortured by C.I.A. interrogators. No lawyers. No right to remain silent. No Geneva Conventions.

Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, who would later be accused of devising the plot, was stripped naked, rectally abused and waterboarded 183 times. A psychologist threatened to kill his son if more children died in attacks by Al Qaeda.

The agency kept its captives in solitary confinement as it questioned them hundreds of times, effectively training them to believe that if they did not talk, they would be tortured more.

Now, 25 years later, the costs and trade-offs made then are still reverberating in the agonizing wait for a trial in a faraway military court where the legacy of torture hangs over the Sept. 11 case.

Military judges have now thrown out all of the key confessions in the death penalty cases at Guantánamo Bay because the defendants were tortured by the C.I.A.

The fifth and final ruling came early last month. Within weeks, the Supreme Court declined to review a plea deal between prosecutors and Mr. Mohammed and two others accused of conspiracy in the case. The prisoners would have received life sentences in exchange for publicly admitting to their specific roles in the plot.

.

Could this be a turning point for the Sept. 11 families who have waited so long for a day of reckoning? The judge recently set a June 5, 2028, trial date.

“I do think it’s an important moment,” said Jessica Trant, whose father, Dan, a bond trader, was killed at the World Trade Center. “A trial would at least give us the chance to hear the evidence, confront what happened and maybe take back a little of the power we’ve lost along the way.”

That said, Ms. Trant added: “I also know that just because we’re moving toward a trial doesn’t mean we’ll actually get one.”

John Ryan, a former task force commander at ground zero and chief of the Port Authority Police, said two years was too long to wait. He worries that lawyers who have been serving on the case as capital defenders could age out, or another issue could emerge.

“Let’s move the trial date up so that no unforeseen issues can surface,” he said. “This would also support the elder family members who want to see justice in their lifetimes.”

But the other death penalty case at Guantánamo is going first: Jury selection began last month in the trial of a Saudi man who is accused of having a key role in the suicide bombing of a U.S. Navy warship in a harbor in Yemen on Oct. 12, 2000. Seventeen U.S. sailors were killed in the Qaeda attack, and dozens more were wounded.

Hearings in that case recently focused on whether the defendant, Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, is too damaged by his torture while he was in C.I.A. custody from 2002 to 2006 to go to trial.

Here is a look at five fateful decisions that led to this day.

Mr. Mohammed was captured in Pakistan in March 2003 and taken to a secret C.I.A. prison in Poland, called a black site. He was, among other things, waterboarded in a desperate search for the whereabouts of Osama bin Laden and information about other potential sleeper cells and plots.

Call it the original sin. The United States could have transferred him to Guantánamo, where the military was holding about 650 detainees from more than 40 countries at the time.

Or, he could have been sent to the United States.

“From the very beginning he said, ‘Take me to New York, give me a lawyer and I’ll be happy to talk to you,’” Rita Radostitz, one of his lawyers, said in court in September 2021. “But instead of doing that, instead of taking him up on that offer, the government made a choice to take a different path.”

But the C.I.A. cannot operate on U.S. soil.

The United States took him on a three-and-a-half-year odyssey through U.S.-controlled prisons from Eastern Europe to Afghanistan, where he was held incommunicado and, according to his lawyer, questioned hundreds of times, sometimes three times a day.

By 2006 the existence of the once-secret prison system had been revealed, and Mr. Bush had the defendants transferred to Guantánamo for trial.

But there was a problem. What the prisoners had told U.S. interrogators hundreds of times in the black sites was undeniably coerced and would be inadmissible at any U.S. court.

Putting them on trial, Bush administration lawyers decided, would require new evidence. So federal agents called “clean teams” were summoned to Guantánamo to obtain fresh confessions.

This time, in January 2007, the prisoners were told their participation was voluntary.

The prisoners were taken in blindfolds and shackles to a former C.I.A. black site at Guantánamo for questioning. The Bush administration also chose to omit a few key components: The prisoners still had not been allowed to consult lawyers, and they were not told that their hundreds of previous statements could not be used against them.

These decisions would prove catastrophic two decades later.

Hearings in the case of Mr. Mohammed and four other men also accused of conspiracy had barely begun when Barack Obama was elected in 2008. The new president suspended the proceedings at Guantánamo.

Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. announced, after a period of analysis, that the Obama administration had chosen to put the Sept. 11 defendants on trial in federal civilian court in New York.

The Obama administration did not immediately transfer the defendants to New York or any other trial venue, even as civilian prosecutors concluded they could not use the so-called clean-team confessions.

The federal prosecutors thought they would be inadmissible because the agents who questioned the men at Guantánamo had not read them a Miranda warning.

The decision to try the men in New York had led to a political outcry, and Congress forbade the use of federal funds to transfer them to the United States for trial.

The case was returned to Guantánamo, and military prosecutors chose a different path. They would seek to use the clean-team confessions — which have now been rejected by three military judges and a military court of appeals because of the prisoners’ years of torture and isolation.

Still bitter in 2024, Mr. Holder blamed “the politicians and hacks who second-guessed my decision to bring cases in the effective federal courts.” He said, “Had it not been for their political machinations, Khalid Shaikh Mohammed would just be a bad memory now.”

In 2018 the first military judge in the case, Col. James L. Pohl of the Army, suppressed the clean-team confessions of the then-five defendants in the Sept. 11 case. (Since then, one was found to be mentally unfit to face trial.)The judge ruled that a framework set up by prosecutors to protect C.I.A. secrets was unfair. The information provided to the defense lawyers, the judge ruled, denied them the “particularity and nuance necessary to present a rich and vivid account of the 3-to-4-year period in C.I.A. custody.”

Prosecutors appealed, declaring the 2007 statements crucial capital trial evidence. Years of litigation examined the C.I.A. program of violence and isolation, culminating last month with the military judge throwing out the statements of the fourth and final Sept. 11 defendant.

In the summer of 2024, Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III withdrew from plea agreements that prosecutors had said were “the best path to finality and justice in this case.”

Prosecutors had not so secretly negotiated for years with Mr. Mohammed and two other defendants. In exchange for life sentences, the defendants would openly admit to their specific roles in the hijacking plot that killed 2,976 people and give up nearly every avenue of post-conviction appeal.

Prosecutors would present their case to a military jury. The prisoners agreed to answer written questions from relatives of the dead through a process known as restorative justice.

But Mr. Austin said he was unaware of the deal and chose to revoke it.

That decision led to two more years of litigation. Lower courts ruled that Mr. Austin acted too late to withdraw from the contract; then a civilian court ruled that he had the power to do it. On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court decided not to second-guess Mr. Austin’s authority to make that decision.

For now, the trial of Mr. Mohammed and the others is on track to start on June 5, 2028. Tom Resta has gone to Guantánamo four times to watch the proceedings and has no faith that the trial date will hold.

“We were supposed to have a trial starting in 2021,” said Mr. Resta, whose brother John and sister-in-law Sylvia were killed at the World Trade Center. She was seven months pregnant.

item.title: Want to Short a Stock? You Can Do It on Kalshi, at Least for Now.
item.description:
In late April, Kalshi, the world’s largest prediction market, invited a big crowd to a posh event to launch a new type of trading that would allow customers to wager on cryptocurrencies they did not own.

This type of trading had never before been permitted in the United States. But Kalshi was so confident that it would win approval from its regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, that it booked the event before it had even put in its formal application. After all, the agency’s chairman, Michael S. Selig, had repeatedly signaled that he was a prediction markets booster.

When the C.F.T.C. did not move fast enough, Kalshi was forced to cancel the gathering at a glass-domed Brooklyn penthouse with sweeping views of the Manhattan skyline. And the firm’s chief executive, Tarek Mansour, called Mr. Selig to complain, according to three people with knowledge of the call who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private conversation.

But Kalshi just needed to be patient. Mr. Selig’s support was never in question.

In a series of decisions from May onward, he reversed years of agency policy and gave Kalshi what it wanted: permission to let customers bet on the prices of individual stocks, cryptocurrencies or other assets without buying them or being forced to settle up by a specific date. Now, for example, clients could simply wager that the price of shares of ExxonMobil would fall and then get paid if it did.

It was the first time the trades, called perpetuals, were permitted to be offered to American customers. And the agency’s authorizations immediately infuriated officials at some of the nation’s largest trading exchanges who saw Kalshi as a privileged new competitor.

Two powerful clearinghouses — the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and Cboe Global Markets — have filed suit against the agency, claiming that giving prediction markets this leeway violates federal laws designed to protect investors from insider trading, market manipulation and other abuses.

Lawsuits brought by major trading clearinghouses against their own regulator are extremely rare, partly for fear of repercussions. Nasdaq, one of the nation’s leading stock exchanges, has also publicly objected to perpetuals trading but has not filed suit.

The C.F.T.C. turnabout is one of a string of actions benefiting prediction markets, a fast-growing business sector that President Trump enthusiastically supports, and in which his oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., has a financial stake worth millions. The authorizations also help the cryptocurrency industry in which the Trump family is heavily invested.

The agency has also mounted legal challenges this year against both red and blue states that claim prediction markets are evading state regulations on sports betting, a battle that many expect to end up in the Supreme Court.

“The C.F.T.C. is proving eager to push the envelope on its own legal interpretations, and frankly partner with its own regulated entities” to avoid both securities laws and state regulators, said Tyler Gellasch, who leads Healthy Markets Association, a nonprofit organization that focuses on financial policy.

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

Mr. Selig, who is currently the C.F.T.C.’s sole commissioner, has said that customers are seeking perpetual trades and that Americans should not be “forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues” to conduct them.

“Fearing change, Cboe and other incumbents have decided to take frivolous legal action by attempting to undermine the administration’s pro-innovation agenda,” the agency’s spokeswoman said in an email.

Mr. Mansour, Kalshi’s co-founder, promotes perpetual trades as the most flexible financial instrument ever invented, one that will help his firm develop from a betting platform into a full-service financial exchange. Prediction markets are especially keen to expand their products in case the courts impose restrictions on sports betting, the source of most of their revenue.

In a statement, Kalshi said the lawsuits over perpetual trading were merely “a tool for the current winners to prevent competition and protect the sweet deal they have going: Whether it’s sports books, options, futures or stocks, it’s all about keeping their market share.”

Perpetuals, or “perps” for short, were initially popularized outside the United States partly by Samuel Bankman-Fried, the convicted fraudster who offered such trades for cryptocurrencies on his former trading platform FTX before its spectacular collapse in 2022. The trades also took off on Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange whose founder pleaded guilty to violating an anti-money laundering law, then was pardoned by Mr. Trump a year ago.

Crypto firms pushed hard to legalize such trading in the United States, and Mr. Selig embraced their argument as soon as he was appointed last December. He has said perpetuals would further the president’s goal of making America “the crypto capital of the world.”

Platforms like Kalshi use periodic payments between the traders who bet an asset will go up and those who bet it will go down to keep the contract price in line with the actual market price. Because traders tend to jump in and out of such contracts as the prices fluctuates, they can be highly lucrative for platforms that charge a fee for each transaction.

Before Mr. Selig authorized Kalshi, Coinbase and another crypto firm to offer such trades, his agency had pressed civil charges against firms like Binance for doing so.

Perpetual trades on stocks are in some ways like stock options, where ordinary investors can gain the right to buy or sell an individual stock at a certain price on or before a certain date.

But those investors have a wealth of protections that opponents say are much diminished for perpetual traders. For instance, stock options are traded through broker-dealers, creating an audit trail, and monitored through the surveillance system of the Securities and Exchange Commission.

While Kalshi has also registered with the S.E.C. as an exchange, the C.F.T.C. is acting as the primary regulator for perpetual trades. It generally oversees futures and commodities markets that professional traders use to hedge risk, not financial tools for individual investors, like the S.E.C.

The traditional trading exchanges argue that the prediction markets are setting up a kind of shadow stock market that puts investors, and potentially the broader financial markets, at risk.

“We certainly don’t want to see public customers be negatively impacted because of a lack of customer protection that the securities laws in particular are specifically designed to address,” Craig Donohue, Cboe’s chief executive officer, said in an interview last week.

Terrence A. Duffy, the chairman of the C.M.E. Group, which runs the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, has been especially vocal in his criticism of the C.F.T.C.

“It does feel a bit of a ready, fire, aim strategy going on right now where anything can go, and so it’s very disconcerting,” he said on a Bloomberg podcast in October. “They are circumventing basically acts of Congress.”

In closed-door meetings, some career officials at the S.E.C. voiced concerns that the C.F.T.C. was skirting securities laws, according to three people familiar with the situation who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe internal government deliberations. A spokesman for the S.E.C. said the agency “supports bringing previously unavailable products to the U.S. markets within a framework of comprehensive oversight.”

Cboe made some initial headway after it sued in federal court last week over perpetual trades on stocks. A federal judge ruled that the exchange was likely to prevail with its claim that the C.F.T.C. had exceeded its statutory authority. Citadel Securities, Healthy Markets and other broker-dealers and exchanges are also plaintiffs.

“The C.F.T.C.’s actions seem to represent a major disruption to the equities market, and the public, including plaintiff, would be served by preventing such a disruption before it occurs,” wrote Judge Valerie Caproni of Federal District Court for the Southern District of New York.

The agency could also face scrutiny from the Senate Banking Committee. Come January, it is set to be led by Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts. Last week, she said perpetuals trades are highly risky and accused the C.F.T.C. of “rubber-stamping 24/7 high-stakes gambling on our stock market.”

The C.F.T.C. and the prediction markets claim such protests are vastly overblown. They say the agency is acting within its powers and protecting traders and markets with strong rules, surveillance and enforcement.

Kalshi officials say that perpetual trades are no more risky than any other betting on predictions markets, such as how a particular sports team will perform or who will leave the Trump administration before the end of the year. They contend that these trades are more flexible and cheaper than traditional trades like stock options.

The C.F.T.C. is also permitting Kalshi to list other types of stock-related trades, including bets on how the stock market indexes like the Nasdaq 100 will perform and on key corporate indicators that help drive individual stock prices. For example, traders can bet on the amount of sales McDonald’s Corporation will report or how many commercial airlines Boeing will deliver during a certain period.

Kalshi is now offering perpetual trades on at least 50 individual stocks, including some of the country’s biggest companies, such as Google, Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft and Amazon. Since the C.F.T.C. authorized the product on Nov. 3, the platform says it has seen particularly brisk trading volume, amounting to billions of dollars.

“Stock market exposure is the next step towards Kalshi becoming a full-service financial exchange, and perps are the best way for our traders to get this exposure,” Mr. Mansour said last month.

item.title: Why New England’s Republican Governors Withstood the Blue Wave
item.description:
Peter Gallagher, a voter in liberal Townshend, Vt., filled in the ovals for Democrat after Democrat at the polls last Tuesday. But when it came to the race for governor, Mr. Gallagher, 67, made a notable exception: He voted for the Republican incumbent, Gov. Phil Scott.

So did Joanne Davis of Putney, who said she appreciated Mr. Scott’s low-key persona: “He’s a normal person. Not crazy, not scary.”

Vermont voters helped drive the blue wave that stunned the country, casting out two dozen Republicans from the state Legislature and replacing them with Democrats, who regained supermajorities in both chambers. But enough also stuck by Mr. Scott, a soft-spoken moderate, to deliver him a record sixth term, in a state that favored Vice President Kamala Harris over President Trump in 2024 by one of the widest margins in the country.

Mr. Scott’s success in a liberal New England state — and the success of Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who was re-elected last week in neighboring New Hampshire — offer a glimmer of hope for a party freshly battered by rejection. In different ways, the two governors have survived by leaning into an old-school strain of Republicanism, melding fiscal pragmatism with a moderate approach on social issues. Mr. Scott, in particular, has also explicitly separated himself from President Trump.

“He’s the only Republican I’ve ever voted for,” Mr. Gallagher said of Mr. Scott as he loaded groceries into his car outside a supermarket in Brattleboro, Vt., last week. “I like the way he crosses the aisle and works with people — that’s the biggest thing.”

Both governors fit a prototype with deep roots in New England, a region better known for liberalism. In Massachusetts, voters have frequently sought to keep liberal legislators in check by electing moderate Republican governors like William Weld and Charlie Baker.

New Hampshire was long known for a “leave-us-alone type of Republican, with a kind of libertarian flavor to it, and a focus on the small footprint of government,” said Dante Scala, a professor of political science at the University of New Hampshire.

As the national Republican Party shifted toward a new model over the last half century, courting socially conservative and religious voters, the influence of New England’s fiscal conservatives waned, he said. Now, the moderate, compromise-seeking approach modeled by Mr. Scott and Ms. Ayotte may gain new national relevance.

Ms. Ayotte, who was first elected governor in 2024, appears to have endured in part by showing restraint on social issues that Republicans elsewhere have gone to battle over. She vetoed legislation this year that would have rolled back discrimination protections for transgender people. And she has kept a campaign promise to leave New Hampshire’s relatively permissive abortion laws alone.

“She said she would put those issues on the back burner as governor, and she has done that,” Dr. Scala said. “It’s a key question for the Republican Party, whether they continue to put culture wars and social issues at the center of the party’s future identity.”

Both Ms. Ayotte and Mr. Scott faced serious challenges this year from Democrats whose campaigns gained unexpected momentum as the national mood turned against incumbents. Ms. Ayotte won, 51 to 47 percent, after hammering her opponent, Cinde Warmington, for her brief stint as a pharmaceutical lobbyist. In Vermont, Mr. Scott won, 52 to 46 percent, — the closest race of the six he has run for governor, against Amanda Janoo, a progressive Democrat.

New Hampshire and Vermont are the only states in the country where governors’ terms are two years instead of four.

Ms Janoo, in her first run for office, won 71 percent of votes in the state’s largest city, Burlington. One of her main proposals was to raise taxes on Vermont’s highest earners to help pay for universal primary health care. Mr. Scott, who called for cutting taxes, won by a similarly wide margin in the state’s traditional Republican strongholds: its rural western edge and towns along its remote northern border.

Ms. Janoo, whose background is in economics, argued that Mr. Scott’s trickle-down model had failed to deliver on affordability, and proposed that the state instead “build its economy from the bottom up” rather than relying on outside investors.

But even some Vermont voters who longed for change gravitated back to the familiar instead. Michelle Mortimer, a registered nurse and small business owner from Williamsville, felt that Mr. Scott had served long enough. She watched three debates, hoping to be persuaded that Ms. Janoo had a solid plan to rein in health care costs.

“I was begging her to say something to make me vote for her, but she had nothing concrete,” said Ms. Mortimer, 56, who ended up voting for Mr. Scott. “Her answers were soft and squishy.”

Mr. Scott was also helped by voters like Anne Wheeler, 44, of Putney, who until last week had never voted for him. Ms. Wheeler, who works in a factory doing quality control, said she voted for Mr. Scott out of frustration with the state’s high cost of living. She increasingly believes that “progressive liberals are hurting, not helping, Vermont.”

“Vermont is only for the rich or poor,” she said outside the grocery store in Brattleboro. “There are no jobs or housing for the working class. It’s getting harder and harder to stay here — I don’t want to work two or three jobs to survive.”

Mr. Scott has long talked about affordability, and he blamed rising taxes on the Democrat-controlled legislature. Voters rebelled two years ago, ousting two dozen Democrats in the wake of a staggering property tax increase. Last week, they reinstated many of the same Democrats.

The governor’s bipartisan appeal dates to his early days in state government, said Paul Dame, chairman of the Vermont Republican Party. Mr. Scott was elected lieutenant governor in 2010, and served under Gov. Peter Shumlin, a Democrat.

His understated manner, and roots in blue-collar Barre, made Mr. Scott a natural choice for working-class voters. So did his weekend passion for stock car racing and his winning record at the Thunder Road racetrack in Barre.

“While the Democratic Party was becoming more elite, he was connecting with working-class Democrats and building that coalition,” said Mr. Dame.

Mr. Scott also let it be known that he voted for President Biden in 2020 and for Ms. Harris in 2024. But he did so without drama. “He doesn’t go on cable news shows,” said Jason Maulucci, his policy director and campaign manager. “He doesn’t go out of his way to antagonize or attack. People in Vermont value that.”

(Mr. Scott did not commit to an interview for this article; Ms. Ayotte did not respond to requests for comment.)

Mr. Scott’s brand — unflashy dependability — is not exciting. But he leaned into his image as “Governor Dad,” as some have called him, during the campaign, warning voters that the last two years of the Trump administration would be “incredibly chaotic” and asking them: “Who do you want at the wheel?”

Even as she made the case for change, Ms. Janoo recognized the tempting solace of the status quo.

“I think we’re all pretty traumatized,” she said on Wednesday. “In that context, I understand holding onto what feels secure.”

item.title: At a Civil Rights Landmark, a Night of Jubilation Over Colom’s Victory
item.description:
On the lawn of Tougaloo College, steps from the chapel where the civil rights leaders Fannie Lou Hamer and Medgar Evers gave speeches, they danced.

Students from Tougaloo and other nearby historically Black institutions lined the sidewalk to cheer and applaud. Members of Black fraternities and sororities, dressed in their letters and colors, embraced one another. “Thank the Lord, we did it,” one woman declared.

It was a day that many had prayed would come, though they could never know when. That evening, Scott Colom made their hopes a reality, speaking in front of the college chapel as the senator-elect from Mississippi.

Tyler Dotson, 21, a freshman at Tougaloo College, was awe-struck. “It was everything,” he said, describing how it felt to hear that Mr. Colom had won. “We’ve been waiting a long time.”

“It’s something big, remembered in history,” he added, grinning. “We back.”

When the U.S. Senate race in Mississippi was called for Mr. Colom, who will become the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era, shouts of celebration erupted at the local N.A.A.C.P. office.

At a law office in Jackson, everyone stopped working and screamed for joy.

At Tougaloo, the rows of chairs filled long before the victory speech began, as hundreds gathered at the college that had been both a haven and a proving ground for a generation of civil rights activists and Black leaders.

It had been eight days since the election. It had been 63 years since Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who led voting rights drives in the state, was assassinated in his driveway. And it had been more than 150 years since a Black senator had been chosen to represent Mississippi.

For generations, Mississippi was a bastion of slavery, segregation, lynching and Black voter suppression.

Mr. Colom will be the third Black senator to represent the state. The first two were chosen by the state legislature and served during Reconstruction — Mr. Colom will be the first chosen by voters.

“It lets me know that my work isn’t in vain,” said Jermarius Everett, 20, wearing a black and gold jacket of Alpha Phi Alpha, the fraternity to which Mr. Colom also belongs. “I can sit in the seats that once controlled people like me.”

Some in Mississippi, including Nadia Colom, Mr. Colom’s wife, pointed to President Barack Obama’s election in 2008 as the last moment where this kind of hope reverberated through their communities.

At a bar in downtown Jackson, Robert Morris, 37, sat on the patio and said the Senate election had made history he never expected to witness as a lifelong resident of the Deep South.

“I never thought I’d see a Black president, never thought I’d see a Black senator, especially a Black senator from Mississippi,” Mr. Morris said. “Remember when André 3000 said the South has something to say? Well, now Mississippi does. Everybody is paying attention to us, and we’re going to do things right.”

Many college-educated residents of Mississippi have left the state over the years to seek jobs and more progressive environments elsewhere. Terry Rogers II, a 21-year-old senior studying political science at Tougaloo, said Mr. Colom’s win could help change that.

“This is what we’ve been praying for, for years, for generations,” he said. Mr. Rogers had spent Tuesday driving a college van to shuttle students between government offices to check on their ballots as the race remained uncalled. “This makes me want to continue to be a Mississippian. This makes me love my state even more than I already did.”

As Mr. Rogers spoke, another student shouted in joyous disbelief: “He won! You see that? You see that?”

Many voters brought along the next generation, eager to help them absorb the moment.

“I don’t have the words to describe the joy,” said Lisa Ross, 63, a lawyer in Jackson. She brought her great-niece and great-nephew to Tougaloo College, “to see Scott and what they can become.”

“We’ve been working so hard, and I’m so glad we didn’t give up,” she said.

Vonda Reeves, 68, a doctor in Jackson, learned of Mr. Colom’s win during a break in her tennis lesson. Then, she said, “the world exploded. Everything became surreal to me.”

“It was like I was levitating because of the joy I felt,” Dr. Reeves said, adding that she wished her parents had been there to see the milestone.

The celebration reflected the coalition that Mr. Colom had built: not just the Black voters enraged by efforts to undermine their voting power and their representation, but the white Democrats who had hoped that their political drought could end with Mr. Colom.

Mary Evelyn Dear, 32, had never been to Tougaloo College and hesitated to go alone. But she dabbed some glitter around the corners of her eyes and drove over, unwilling to miss the moment.

“I wanted this to happen so badly — it’s part of history,” said Ms. Dear, who is white. She jumped on her couch and shrieked with joy after days of refreshing the ballot totals over and over again.

Many leaders saw Mr. Colom’s win as a poignant triumph for voting rights.

“Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out,” said Derrick Johnson, the national president of the N.A.A.C.P., in a statement. This year, the N.A.A.C.P. opened 11 field offices and registered more than 17,000 voters, he added. The Jackson office still has bullet holes from the time Mr. Evers worked in the state, when he faced several assassination attempts before being killed in his own driveway.

Reginald Crear, 45, had grown up hearing his father’s stories about the Jim Crow era in Mississippi. On Wednesday, he had his father on a video call so he could watch Mr. Colom’s speech with him.

“It really gives me goose bumps,” he said, adding “it was surreal, a real surreal moment.”

Amid the exuberant celebrations, Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party, said in a statement, “Scott Colom ran a good campaign here in Mississippi, and I congratulate him on his victory.”

He continued: “While elections may determine who holds public office, they do not define who we are as a people nor diminish the principles we hold dear. Tomorrow, the sun will rise over the same Mississippi we loved yesterday.”

Nsombi Lambright, 53, was at the local N.A.A.C.P. office when the news broke that Mr. Colom had won. People began singing “We Shall Overcome,” the civil rights anthem, and started hugging and crying. She wore a shirt with a picture of Emmett Till, the 14-year-old boy lynched in Mississippi in 1955.

“We have felt really beat up over the last year,” she said, pointing to the deaths of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old found dead after a boat trip with friends, and Kohen Wiley, the toddler shot and killed by a police officer, as examples of events that had shaken Black Mississippians this year. “We needed this.”

Michael Goldberg, the Politics reporter for Mississippi Today, contributed reporting from Jackson.

item.title: 5 People Are Shot in Washington, D.C., Officials Say
item.description:
Five people were shot near a busy area of Washington, D.C., on Thursday, the D.C. police said, prompting a widespread law enforcement response in the Logan Circle neighborhood.

A suspected shooter was barricaded in a building in the 1500 block of 15th Street, the authorities said. The number of people shot and their condition were not immediately known.

The shooting took place in the area of 15th and P Street, the police said. The Logan Circle area where it occurred is a residential neighborhood less than a mile from the White House and home to coffee shops and other businesses.

The New York Times

The gunfire was outside VIDA, a gym in the neighborhood, said Brooke Pinto, a member of Washington’s city council, in a post on social media.

Near the site of the shooting, dozens of police and law enforcement vehicles blocked the streets, including several SWAT vehicles. An emergency alert to cellphones in the area instructed people to shelter in place.

Helicopters circled overhead as ambulances arrived at the scene.

Phil Morton, 37, said he had just arrived at work for the day when he heard a “parade of police cars” and screeching tires outside his office.

Mr. Morton, a vehicle safety engineer, said he initially thought the ruckus might be a presidential motorcade.

On the street, Mr. Morton said it was “madness,” adding that he saw a large police presence and officers with long guns. The scene had quieted a little by 9:30 a.m., but the several blocks around the area were still cordoned off, he said.

The area around the VIDA gym is a quiet intersection of streets downtown, with restaurants, a church and an elementary school nearby.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Trump Says He’s Pulling Vance Off Iran Talks to Focus on Fraud Campaign
item.description:
President Trump said on Thursday that he had pulled Vice President JD Vance back from engaging in potential peace talks with Iran, saying that his time would be better spent investigating fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media. “Those days have long since passed.”

The post deepens questions about what Mr. Trump’s plan is to end the war. The president has been weighing a number of options, including ramping up military strikes, withdrawing and leaving the matter to Arab allies or simply maintaining the status quo.

It also signals a pivot on his instructions to Mr. Vance, after the vice president publicly blamed the war for the Republican Party’s devastating midterm election losses.

Mr. Trump had assigned Mr. Vance, who privately expressed opposition to going to war with Iran, to lead negotiations earlier this year. The vice president traveled to Pakistan in April and met with Iranian leaders in a marathon session that ended without any resolution.

Mr. Vance recently contacted a top Iranian political and military official to propose a renewal of comprehensive peace negotiations. In a letter sent from Mr. Vance via Qatari meditators to Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and former commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, the vice president suggested that American and Iranian officials meet soon, adding that he would lead the talks for the United States.

But Mr. Trump said on Thursday that he was ending that effort.

“I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.,” he wrote on social media.

While there is a high-profile fraud investigation in Minnesota that has resulted in scores of arrests, federal data does not support the president’s suggestion that fraud occurs more prevalently under Democrats than Republicans. Mr. Trump has also granted clemency to more than 70 allies, donors and others convicted in fraud cases, often involved high-dollar totals.

item.title: The Concession Call to an Election Winner Is No Longer a Given
item.description:
When the campaign trail runs out, the concession call is a tradition that is excruciating for the loser and sweet for the victor.

If it happens at all.

Last week, Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected Democratic senator from Michigan, said that his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, had never called.

“At the end of the day, it really doesn’t quite matter,” Mr. El-Sayed told reporters. “I’m sure he had a flight to catch to Florida,” a reference to Mr. Rogers owning a second home near Fort Myers. (A spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers did not reply to a request for comment.)

Amy Acton, who was elected Ohio’s governor, said she had refused to take a call from Vivek Ramaswamy, her vanquished Republican rival, who in the final weeks of the campaign featured Ms. Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar in a TV commercial. Mr. Ramaswamy said in his concession speech that he had called Ms. Acton and left a message congratulating her.

“I have no intention of speaking to him,” Ms. Acton told “CBS Mornings” last week. “I do believe that leaders’ words matter.”

In a bygone era, such breaches of political protocol might have been unheard of. Yet as the 2026 midterm elections wind down, with several House races and a Senate race in Alaska too close to call, one might conclude that failing to concede defeat is more frequent than ever, the latest norm of polite politics to become a casualty of a less civil age.

Historically, concessions in American politics have come in two prongs: a personal communication between candidates, as well as a public speech. And some candidates still appear to embrace those customs.

On Wednesday, Rep. Mike Lawler, Republican of New York, posted a picture on X with Cait Conley, the Democrat who had just unseated him, in spite of the acrimony of their campaign. “We had a great conversation about the district, the work ahead and our mutual respect for each other,” Mr. Lawler wrote. “I wish Cait well as she takes up the mantle.”

And when Scott Colom’s upset in Mississippi was announced Wednesday evening, it was met by well wishes in a concession video from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican.

A message of concession is “the single most important thing that happens in an election,” said Scott Farris, who wrote the book “Almost President: The Men Who Lost the Race but Changed the Nation.” In Mr. Farris’s own unsuccessful 1998 run for Congress in Wyoming, he did not make a concession call. He quickly regretted it — and later agreed to appear at a joint luncheon with his winning opponent, Barbara Cubin.

“We have this metaphor of politics as a war. And so when the war is over, people want it to be over. They don’t want it to keep having guerrilla warfare,” Mr. Farris said. “So they want a definitive surrender, but then they want the victor to also be gracious.”

A laying down of arms was on display in 1948 when Thomas E. Dewey, the New York governor, lost to President Harry S. Truman.

“My heartiest congratulations on your election and every good wish for a successful administration,” Dewey wrote to Truman in a telegram. “I urge all Americans to unite behind you in support of every effort to keep our nation strong and free and to establish peace in the world.”

Dewey did not show the same spirit of reconciliation when he lost the 1944 campaign to President Franklin D. Roosevelt. He was the only presidential loser between 1896 and 1980 not to send a congratulatory telegram to the winner.

Telegrams — first used in the 1896 presidential race — gave way to the telephone in 1980 when President Jimmy Carter called Ronald Reagan. Mr. Carter told supporters in the concession speech that followed that he had congratulated Mr. Reagan “for a fine victory” and promised an orderly transition.

Even after the fierce 2016 election, President-elect Donald J. Trump received a call from Hillary Clinton, which she described in her memoir as “without a doubt one of the strangest moments of my life.”

“I congratulated Trump and offered to do anything I could to make sure the transition was smooth,” she wrote. “It was all perfectly nice and weirdly ordinary, like calling a neighbor to say you can’t make it to his barbecue. It was mercifully brief.”

By 2020, that neighborly spirit had faded when Mr. Trump lost the popular vote and the Electoral College to Joseph R. Biden Jr.

Mr. Trump never admitted that he lost, becoming the first U.S. presidential candidate to refuse to concede in the modern political era. That decision played a part in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol and ushered in a new era of election denialism. (A stark contrast with the conciliatory note Mr. Trump left for Mr. Biden in the Oval Office, according to Mr. Biden’s new book.)

In races farther down the ticket and in nonpresidential elections, the tradition of burying the hatchet has usually been kept.

Howard Dean, the former governor of Vermont who sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2004, never made a concession call in his political career. But he received several concessions he remembered in an interview as “cordial” and “pro forma.”

“‘You ran a great race. Thanks very much,’” Mr. Dean said. “I’m, of course, hopefully equally gracious and saying, ‘I really appreciated all your ideas and so forth and so on.’ Hopefully it’s two people being as gracious as they can to be.”

Mitt Romney, who lost the 2012 election to President Barack Obama, wrote in a text message that his concession to Mr. Obama was “not a hard call at all.”

“I had long ago learned that that’s the nature of politics, business, sport, and life,” Mr. Romney said. “I congratulated him: He had run an effective campaign.”

Mr. Romney used a tennis analogy.

“If you’re playing in the U.S. Open and your opponent serves an ace, you congratulate him,” he said.

Not all calls go smoothly. Political history’s most famous concession call — or calls — occurred during the 2000 election. At first, then-Vice President Al Gore conceded to Gov. George W. Bush of Texas. But as Florida’s narrowing margins brought the results into question, Mr. Gore called to take it back.

“You mean to tell me, Mr. Vice President, you’re retracting your concession?” a stunned Mr. Bush said.

Mr. Gore responded: “You don’t have to be snippy about it.”

Eventually, Mr. Gore would concede again.

But he did it in a speech, and quipped that he wouldn’t be calling Mr. Bush for a third time.

Losing feels terrible, especially after a rough campaign. When Jaime Harrison failed in 2020 in South Carolina to unseat Senator Lindsey Graham, he said in an interview, he “felt like crap.” That didn’t stop him from aiming for magnanimity in his concession.

“Leaders have to lead,” Mr. Harrison said. “And even in times when they’re frustrated or times in which they’re upset, and times when they hurt.”

item.title: Will the Supreme Court Thwart Congressional Investigations?
item.description:
Come January, a Congress newly dominated by Democrats will launch vigorous investigations of the Trump administration and its allies.

Lawmakers will face a target-rich environment, one that includes crypto deals, pardons, extrajudicial killings on the high seas, a Justice Department-led retribution campaign against the president’s political opponents, and the gift of a Qatari jet.

But they will also face hurdles and roadblocks — erected by the Supreme Court.

In the court’s 2024 decision granting President Trump substantial immunity from prosecution, Chief Justice John Roberts indicated that some subjects may be entirely off limits to congressional investigators.

“Congress cannot act on, and courts cannot examine, the president’s actions on subjects within his ‘conclusive and preclusive’ constitutional authority,” the chief justice wrote. Those subjects included issuing pardons, firing subordinates and deciding “which crimes to investigate and prosecute.”

The immunity decision “has quietly weakened Congress’s ability to conduct legislative oversight over the executive branch,” David Manners-Weber wrote on the Lawfare blog just before the midterm elections.

Whatever the subjects of congressional investigations, the administration is unlikely to give Congress documents or let officials testify, a clash that could lead to lawsuits. And it is not at all clear that the Supreme Court would be willing to mediate those disputes, or if the justices would side with the Democratic Congress if it does.

Perhaps surprisingly, the court has never definitively resolved a basic question: Can Congress sue the executive branch?

In 2015, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg noted in passing that “whether Congress has standing to bring a suit against the president” was an open question. “A suit between Congress and the president,” she observed, “would raise separation-of-powers concerns.”

Lower courts have been more receptive to suits from legislators.

In a pair of decisions in 2020, in the waning days of the first Trump administration, the D.C. Circuit ruled that lawsuits could proceed despite objections to the lawmakers’ standing.

In one decision, the court said that the House Judiciary Committee, then led by Democrats, had standing to sue Don McGahn, a former White House counsel, to compel him to testify. In the other, the court allowed the full House of Representatives to sue over Trump’s use of emergency powers to spend more public funds on a border wall than Congress had appropriated.

McGahn and the committee settled their dispute following some additional twists and turns. After the 2020 election, the Biden administration stopped building the border wall, then asked the Supreme Court to wipe out the appeals court’s decision.

The Biden administration, aware of political pendulum swings, sided with the Trump administration and argued that the House alone should not be allowed to sue the president.

Elizabeth Prelogar, the solicitor general under President Joe Biden, told the justices that letting the House sue “would inject the federal courts into fundamentally political disputes and upset the balance of power between the political branches.”

The Supreme Court granted the Biden administration’s petition and vacated the D.C. Circuit’s decision as moot. The court’s brief order said nothing about whether Congress, or parts of it, had standing to sue the executive branch.

I asked Payvand Ahdout, a law professor at the University of Virginia and an authority on inter-branch litigation, for an overview of the likely litigation.

“I largely agree that there are many roadblocks to courts rendering decisions on the merits in any of these cases,” she said in an email. “And even if Congress can overcome those roadblocks, courts frequently engage in avoidance techniques to keep from ordering a coordinate branch of government to take action.”

But she added that “the judiciary is not a monolith” and “we may see some cases where Congress finds an ally in the lower courts that moves the needle for investigations and oversight.”

So far I’ve been discussing clashes between Congress and the executive branch. Lawmakers will probably find it easier to obtain information from private parties like Elon Musk, or the law firms that settled with the administration after threats that they and their clients could lose government contracts.

But even in those kinds of cases, the court has imposed limits on the authority of lawmakers. In 2020, in Trump v. Mazars, the court considered congressional subpoenas seeking Trump’s tax and business records from accounting and financial institutions with which he had done business. Trump sued to block the release of the records.

Returning the case to a lower court for further analysis, Chief Justice Roberts stressed that lawmakers needed “a valid legislative purpose” for seeking the records.

“Congress may not issue a subpoena for the purpose of ‘law enforcement,’” he wrote, quoting , “because ‘those powers are assigned under our Constitution to the executive and the judiciary.’”

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

The ruling was not particularly clear about where to draw the line between the two. In general, the chief justice seemed to prefer accommodation over litigation.

“Historically, disputes over congressional demands for presidential documents have not ended up in court,” he wrote. “Instead, they have been hashed out in the ‘hurly-burly, the give-and-take of the political process between the legislative and the executive.’”

That is, he urged the parties to work out their differences and leave the courts out of it.

The quotation supporting that approach was part of 1975 testimony from a Justice Department lawyer before a Senate committee. The lawyer was Antonin Scalia, who would join the Supreme Court about a decade later.

In the Trump era, the give-and-take Scalia called for seems to have vanished.

The administration has, for instance, taken an extraordinarily broad view of executive privilege, saying it extends to the president’s discussions with people outside the government.

In August, the Office of Legal Counsel, the unit of the Justice Department that advises the executive branch on the law, issued a memorandum making the case for a vast expansion of the scope of executive privilege. It relied heavily on the Mazars decision from 2020, citing it eight times.

Mailbag

If Congress passed a law setting term limits for justices, could the Supreme Court find it unconstitutional? — Barbara Insel

Yes, but it would be awkward. It’s not clear how a challenge to the statute would arise, or whether the justices would recuse themselves in light of the obvious conflict. That decision, in turn, could depend on how lower courts ruled.

As we saw just weeks ago, the court sometimes lets lower-court decisions stand when it cannot muster the required quorum of six justices.

These complications, to say nothing of the Constitution’s text (the justices “shall hold their offices during good behavior”), could suggest that a statute is not the right approach.

The report issued by the Biden-appointed Supreme Court commission said that some of its members had concluded that “the existence of constitutional doubt, as well as the significance and complexity of adopting a system of term limits, are themselves reasons to pursue the reform through constitutional amendment.”

“No matter which way the court came out on the question,” the report added, “these commissioners worry that the court’s legitimacy, or perceptions of its legitimacy, would be undermined.”

I would love to hear your questions on the law, the courts or whatever is on your mind. Send them my way at the-docket@nytimes.com.

Closing Argument

J. Harvie Wilkinson is a respected federal appeals court judge who was appointed by President Ronald Reagan and considered for a seat on the Supreme Court by President George W. Bush.

He is also a former journalist, having served for three years as the editorial page editor of The Norfolk Virginian-Pilot before joining the Justice Department. (That did not stop The Pilot from opposing his nomination in 1983. The paper said that he lacked courtroom experience.)

Judge Wilkinson’s background might have played a role in his opinion Tuesday limiting a court order requiring LinkedIn to turn over the records of journalists for an unidentified news organization that published an article “purporting to describe a top-secret United States military operation in a foreign country.”

The ruling did not identify the article or news organization in question. But parts of it raised the possibility that it involved a New York Times article disclosing a botched military operation in North Korea in 2019.

The government sought 18 months’ worth of information that could, Judge Wilkinson wrote, identify a vast number of confidential sources who had nothing to do with the article in question.

Judge Wilkinson, writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, made clear that he understood reporting.

“Confidentiality of sources is the lifeblood of a free press,” he wrote. “Without confidentiality, press coverage would be pushed in the direction of official handouts and outside sources. Without confidentiality, the ability of journalists to report on events of large importance and governmental behavior of dubious legality and integrity could not help but be hampered.”

He added that such reporting may be all the more urgent these days, and that a free press could not be viewed in isolation.

“Press freedom is among those things viewed by autocrats worldwide as a threat to their grip on power,” he wrote. “Criminal prosecutions freed from partisanship and retribution, a fearless and independent judicial system, and a secure and accessible electoral process all serve to supplement press freedom in distinguishing liberty from oppression.”

The decision was nothing like a complete victory for the journalists. Judge Wilkinson said a trial judge could conclude that some of their records must be disclosed. But he said the government had no “license to round up indiscriminately the identities of confidential and unrelated news gathering sources.”

Please send me your comments on congressional investigations, term limits for Supreme Court justices, confidential sources or anything else at the-docket@nytimes.com. See you next week. — Adam

item.title: Ken and Angela Paxton’s Divorce Is Final, His Lawyer Says

Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, has finalized his divorce with his wife, Angela, who cited his adultery in her divorce petition last year, a lawyer for Mr. Paxton said on Thursday.

Ms. Paxton cited “biblical grounds” in her petition last summer to end her marriage of more than 30 years to Mr. Paxton.

Her filing came just months after Mr. Paxton announced his run for Senate, challenging Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary. Mr. Paxton won the primary but lost by a 12-point margin to a Democrat, James Talarico, in last week's election.

item.title: For Democrats, Economic Populism Is Cutting Through Party Divides
item.description:
Claire Valdez, a democratic socialist assemblywoman from Queens, was listening to a campaign speech by Cait Conley, a centrist Army veteran from the Hudson Valley, when she felt a pang of recognition.

“She was talking about billionaires,” Ms. Valdez, who was elected last week in her solidly Democratic district, recalled of Ms. Conley, who flipped a Republican seat in a conservative-leaning area. “It’s like, this sounds like Bernie 2016.”

Now both women are headed to Congress after a Democratic sweep that handed their party firm control of the House and Senate but quickly gave rise to a debate in their ranks about whether progressives or moderates will have the upper hand in driving the agenda come January.

Unlike in the past, however, members of both factions — centrist Democrats who captured competitive districts and the most liberal members in safe seats — appear to have coalesced around a common theme many of them agree won their party the midterms and should be their focus: economic populism.

The last time Democrats controlled both chambers of Congress, under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., bitter policy disagreements between moderates and progressives over how expansive their legislative plan should be prompted intraparty feuds that threatened to derail their economic agenda.

Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate are already navigating some of those same rifts. Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer, the centrist New York Democrats who are now their party’s leaders in the minority, are facing resistance from the left to their bids to keep the top posts in the majority. Some progressives have demanded that they commit to embracing specific far-reaching policy changes on the heels of overwhelming electoral victories.

But for all of the policy disputes that Democrats will still be forced to confront when they take power in January, there is broad agreement among many of the newly elected members on an agenda focused on cutting costs and combating corruption.

Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine — both left-leaning leaders who won in more competitive states — ran on Medicare for all. Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas, a moderate who prevailed in his Republican-dominated state, campaigned on allowing every American, regardless of age, to join Medicare. In heavily Republican Kansas, Senator-elect Adam Hamilton called for expanding Medicare to cover vision and dental care. Nearly all of them railed against billionaires and corporate greed.

“They say it differently, but they are all on the same theme,” Mr. Schumer said in an interview. “It echoed from one end of the country to the other. It set an echo chamber.”

Voters almost uniformly reported that tackling government corruption was one of their top issues in the midterms. A memo issued by House Democrats’ super PAC after the elections said that in focus groups and interviews, “voters cast blame far and wide” for rising household costs, “from greedy corporations and their wealthy C.E.O.s, to corrupt and conflicted politicians.”

That dynamic has already created some unusual ideological crosscurrents in the party. Representative-elect Sam Forstag of Montana, who flipped a conservative seat, told his constituents in a video recorded during new member orientation in Washington this week that he planned to join both the Blue Dog Coalition — a centrist group traditionally made up of southern Democrats — and the liberal Progressive Caucus, two factions that are often at odds with each other.

“The overlap is, well, giving us the chance to fight for populist economic policies that are actually going to help working people, and finally put us back at the front of the line in terms of who Congress should be working for,” Mr. Forstag said.

The approach is also shaping how newly elected Democrats are thinking about using their oversight power in the new Congress. In the past, the most liberal Democrats have clamored for impeachments to punish misconduct.

Now, even progressives are arguing that their party should train their focus on government and corporate wrongdoing that has driven up costs for Americans.

“We really need to look at any specific instance of corruption that can be tied directly to the material circumstances of working families today,” said Representative-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado, a liberal who won a primary race against a veteran Democratic congresswoman.

“I don’t know necessarily that investigating the Qatari jet has a direct impact to the material circumstances of a working person right now in the country,” Ms. Kiros said, referring to the luxury jet given to President Trump by the Qatari royal family. “But I do think if we talk about the role that some of these health insurance companies have been having in the dramatic continuing rise in health care costs today, the collusion that takes place between the big four meatpacking companies and the rise in groceries and meat specifically, right? These are very specific harms that the American people and the American consumer is facing.”

Those issues may also orient Democrats should they choose to try to dare Mr. Trump to veto affordability legislation — around health care or otherwise — through the budget reconciliation process, which allows a party to circumvent the Senate filibuster when passing bills.

The last time Democrats attempted to pass filibuster-proof domestic policy legislation, when the party had a governing trifecta in 2021 under Mr. Biden, progressives and centrists clashed. Liberals refused to support a bipartisan infrastructure measure prioritized by the moderates until the Senate passed their top priority: a behemoth package to fund climate programs, health care, education and child care.

But with Mr. Trump in the White House, Democrats sound more willing to put aside such disagreements and find measures they can coalesce around and pressure the president to accept.

“People just feel like we’re being scammed all the time, and the quality of the things that we enjoyed is getting worse, and people are getting incredibly rich off of it,” Ms. Valdez said. “Even if we won’t agree 100 percent on the specifics with everyone in our caucus, I think we’ll have a lot of places of agreement in tackling this corporate greed.”

Michael Gold and Carl Hulse contributed reporting.

item.title: Kennedy’s Future: Will Democrats Try to Impeach Him, or Actually Work With Him?
item.description:
Three days after last week’s “blue wave” election, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted a warning on X to anyone suspecting his Make America Healthy Again movement had been weakened. “It’s time to unleash the Kraken,” he wrote.

The phrase, a reference to the 1981 move “Clash of the Titans” that gained currency in 2020 among far-right internet personalities who claimed Democrats stole the election, suggests Mr. Kennedy will fight for his agenda and has no intention of leaving his job despite the defeat of several MAHA-backed candidates.

The question now is whether Democrats will use their new majorities in Congress to try to push him out.

Many want to investigate him, saying his vaccine agenda and handling of measles outbreaks have put American lives at risk. Some, including Senator-elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina, want to impeach him. Senator Angela Alsobrooks, Democrat of Maryland, wants Mr. Kennedy removed, but has not said how.

“The time is now,” Ms. Alsobrooks wrote on X the day after the election. “RFK Jr. must resign or be fired. End of discussion.”

But others want to work with Mr. Kennedy in areas where they can agree. They believe his food and environmental policies, which have run into roadblocks with the Trump White House, have a natural home with Democrats, and they see a chance to win over some of the health-focused coalition that helped propel President Trump to a second term.

Democrats like Representative Chellie Pingree of Maine, a regenerative farmer, and Tim Ryan, a former congressman from Ohio, believe the party should not squander an opportunity to woo MAHA voters on those issues. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, a doctor and former state public health official, has proposed his own MAHA agenda under a different name: Build a Healthier America.

“This makes no sense,” Mr. Ryan wrote in response to Ms. Alsobrooks, adding, “Why wouldn’t we work together to see what wins we can get?”

Emily Hilliard, a spokeswoman for Mr. Kennedy, said the secretary would “continue to serve the American people and welcomes working with all members of Congress to turn shared priorities into lasting MAHA reforms.”

MAHA activists across the political spectrum have soured on the Trump White House for stalling Mr. Kennedy’s effort to regulate ultraprocessed foods. Many so-called MAHA Moms, who believed Mr. Trump when he said he would let Mr. Kennedy “go wild on health,” felt betrayed by the president when he issued an executive order ramping up production of glyphosate, a weedkiller that some scientists link to cancer.

“Women feel like they were lied to,” Alex Clark, a conservative podcaster and MAHA influencer, said in February, after the glyphosate order.

Two prominent MAHA leaders, Vani Hari, a cookbook author and healthy eating activist who calls herself “the Food Babe,” and Zen Honeycutt, an environmental activist who founded the group Moms Across America, are former Democrats who followed Mr. Kennedy into Mr. Trump’s camp. Both say they vote the person, not the party.

“I’m frankly tired of reporters asking me, you know, whether I’m loyal to the Republicans, whether I’m loyal to the Democrats,” said Ms. Hari, who was a delegate for Barack Obama at the 2012 Democratic National Convention. “I’m loyal to my children.”

On the day after the election, Ms. Honeycutt joined a webinar for leaders of MAHA Action, a nonprofit advocacy group that supports Mr. Kennedy. She implored Democrats to join forces with the secretary.

“I just urge every Democrat that is considering working against him to sit down and talk with him,” she said. “I think you’re going to love him. I think you’re going to enjoy working with him.”

The blue wave sent a string of Democratic doctors, scientists and health professionals to Congress, who arrived in Washington for freshman orientation this week. But working with Mr. Kennedy may be a hard sell to many of them.

In the past, most of the doctors in Congress have been Republicans, often self-employed and driven to run by business concerns. The new crop of Democrats with professional health backgrounds are animated by the cost of care, access to treatments and in some cases antipathy toward Mr. Kennedy. Ms. Andrews, the senator-elect from South Carolina, a state hit hard by the measles epidemic, ran on a platform of impeaching Mr. Kennedy.

“He’s a clear and present danger to public health,” Ms. Andrews, a pediatrician, said during the campaign.

After the election, Erik Polyak, the executive director of 314 Action, a political action committee that backs scientists and health professionals who run for public office, predicted a rough road ahead for Mr. Kennedy. “We’re going to see R.F.K. Jr.’s head on a platter,” Mr. Polyak told Politico.

The comment ricocheted across the internet, as news organizations declared that “Dems smell blood” and were “coming for” the health secretary. But in an interview, the founder and president of 314 Action, Shaughnessy Naughton, dismissed Mr. Polyak’s statement. “That is not rhetoric that belongs in this conversation,” she said.

Still, Ms. Naughton, who is a chemist and former congressional candidate from Pennsylvania, saw the election results as a repudiation of Mr. Kennedy’s policies, including his attacks on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health.

“We have been warning Republicans for months that voters were going to hold Republicans responsible for the recklessness of R.F.K. Jr.,” she said.

For the moment, Democrats are more focused on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth than Mr. Kennedy. “I don’t think Democrats can spend their time trying to impeach the entire cabinet, and if there are any impeachments, it should start with Secretary Hegseth,” Ms. Pingree said.

But Mr. Kennedy’s detractors may soon get some ammunition. Early next week, an arm of the World Health Organization is expected to strip the United States of its designation as a nation that has eliminated measles. The disease has killed 11 people in the country since Mr. Kennedy took office.

Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats and is likely to become the next chairman of the Senate health committee, told CNN on Sunday that he is “absolutely open” to impeachment. In a statement to The New York Times on Saturday, Mr. Sanders sidestepped questions about whether he would rather impeach or work with Mr. Kennedy.

“R.F.K. Jr. is, by far, the most dangerous health and human services secretary in our nation’s history,” Mr. Sanders said in the statement, adding that his committee “will hold Secretary Kennedy accountable.”

While the election confirmed the rupture between the MAHA movement and Republicans, paradoxically, Mr. Kennedy’s hand inside the White House may now be strengthened. Last week, Mr. Trump announced that he was replacing his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, who has been accused of blocking some MAHA policies, with Stephen Miller, the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. Mr. Miller’s wife, Katie Miller, was Mr. Kennedy’s spokeswoman during the transition.

“Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration,” Mr. Kennedy wrote on X, in his “unleash the Kraken” post.

Some Kennedy allies are urging the secretary to take advantage of MAHA’s fractured relationship with Republicans, and the switch in the White House leadership, to advance his agenda. Ms. Clark sees two options for Mr. Kennedy. One is to quit, and plan a run for president in 2028. “The other option,” she said, “is to go in, guns a-blazing, I don’t care, I’m going to treat every day like the president is going to fire me.”

Even Tony Lyons, the conservative publisher and close Kennedy ally who runs MAHA Action and its sister political action committee, is noticeably shifting his rhetoric.

Early in the election cycle, Mr. Lyons vowed to raise $100 million to elect “MAHA-aligned, Trump-endorsed” Republicans. The MAHA PAC did help elect one Republican, Julia Letlow, the senator-elect from Louisiana, though she did not flip a seat. She will replace Senator Bill Cassidy, who lost to her in a primary.

But some of the MAHA PAC’s marquee Republican candidates lost last week. They include Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas; Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general who was running for Senate; and Zach Lahn, who hoped to become Iowa’s governor. At the MAHA Action post-election event, Mr. Lyons blamed corporate influence and “Big Food, Big Ag, Big Pharma” for the outcomes.

He did not talk about Trump-endorsed Republicans. “We have the building blocks of an incredibly powerful, independent movement that is beholden to no one,” he said.

Mr. Kennedy seems unbowed. At a MAHA Action party in Washington on Monday night, he was surrounded by fans, jockeying to take selfies; one young woman posed holding a small rabbit. He spoke for about 10 minutes, praising Mr. Miller and Ms. Wiles.

But in addition to criticizing Democrats, Mr. Kennedy also took aim at Republicans, who refused to confirm several Trump health appointees, and suggested he may have a freer hand now that the president’s party is no longer in power.

“Every time I tried to do something robust, I would get calls saying, ‘If you do that, we’re not going to confirm your appointees,’” he said. He added: “The Senate no longer has any leverage over me. And you know, that’s a big deal.”

Dani Blum contributed reporting from Washington.
