item.title: House Passes Competing Veterans Bills in a Fight Over Funding
item.description:
The House on Thursday overwhelmingly passed a multibillion-dollar bill that would fully fund a key retirement benefit for combat-injured veterans with disabilities, but the measure’s fate in Congress was uncertain amid a dispute over how to pay for it.

Republican leaders moved to sidestep the disagreement on Wednesday by speeding through a competing measure before Democrats had a chance to try to defeat it. That bill, the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, addresses the retirement pay change and a wide range of veterans programs, all financed by future cuts in benefits for sleep apnea and tinnitus, two conditions that often afflict combat veterans.

The narrower version that passed on Thursday, by a lopsided vote of 392 to 18, was forced to the floor by Democrats and would omit those cuts. All Democrats and 181 Republicans backed it.

The competing bills each face steep obstacles in the Senate. Senator Jerry Moran, Republican of Kansas and the chairman of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee, said he supported the Republican-led package, whereas Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the committee, said he could not back the proposed benefit cuts.

Central to the dispute is the Maj. Richard Star Act, which would allow veterans who retired because of combat-related disabilities to receive their full retirement pay, rather than having it reduced dollar-for-dollar by their disability benefits, as required by current law.

Veterans groups have long lobbied for the Richard Star Act, but over the years, lawmakers have repeatedly balked at its cost, recently estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be about $12.8 billion over a decade.

House Republicans have argued that pairing the Richard Star Act with the sleep apnea and tinnitus cuts in the broader Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would get the provision across the finish line. But for months, retired service members and some powerful veterans groups blasted the package, saying it pitted veterans with disabilities against one another.

The blowback was forceful enough that Republican leaders, attempting to pass the package over the summer, had to pull it from the floor when it became clear they lacked the votes.

The same leaders were able to push it through on Wednesday only after Democrats failed to notice that Republicans had called a vote on it on the House floor. Waiting only six seconds, during which no Democrat requested a recorded vote, they declared the bill passed on a voice vote — a highly unusual move given the standard House practice of allowing opponents the chance to ask for a recall.

Members of both parties had been uncertain whether a majority of the House would be willing to go on the record supporting a measure that cut future benefits. The voice vote allowed it to pass without any lawmaker having to do so.

Representative Mark Takano of California, the ranking Democrat on the Veterans Affairs Committee, accused Republicans of deceiving Democrats by asking him to leave the House floor to review technical changes to the bill, then calling for its passage when he was not present to demand a roll-call vote.

“Republicans chose yesterday, on Veterans Day of all days, to sneak through the largest cut veterans benefits in history,” he said on Thursday. “They knew they didn’t have the votes to pass their bill. So on a highly partisan vote, they resorted to depriving veterans of the honest, fair and transparent process that they deserve.”

Representative Mike Bost of Illinois, the Republican committee chairman who sponsored the veterans package, denied Mr. Takano’s claim.

“There have been rumors from my Democrat colleagues accusing House Republicans of passing my bill through some backdoor deal,” Mr. Bost said. “Nothing could be further from the truth.”

While many Democrats opposed the Republican bill, Mr. Takano’s competing legislation, a stand-alone version of the Richard Star Act that excluded the sleep apnea and tinnitus cuts, drew substantial Republican backing.

That bill came to the floor after a handful of Republicans joined Democrats in working around Speaker Mike Johnson, signing onto a discharge petition that speeds legislation to the floor if a majority of House members demand it.

Representative Gus Bilirakis of Florida, a Republican who has long pressed for the Richard Star Act, did not sign the discharge petition, but voted in favor of Mr. Takano’s bill.

“I promised Maj. Richard Star that we would do everything we possibly could to get this bill across the finish line,” he said of the bill’s namesake, who before dying in 2021, pushed for the policy change after retiring from the Army because of cancer that he developed in the Middle East.

Representative Maxine Dexter, an Oregon Democrat and physician serving on the Veterans’ Affairs committee, said she had seen too many patients with tinnitus and sleep apnea at Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals to justify the cuts.

“If we are not supporting that for our veterans, I don’t know what in the world we’re doing,” she said. “These are conditions as a result of their service.”

Republican lawmakers have pressed their members to oppose Mr. Takano’s proposal, arguing that benefit cuts would help pay for a more substantial veterans-spending package, which included the Richard Star Act. The Republican package would fund dozens of other veterans programs, from expansion of mental health care benefits to service dogs.

Representative Dan Crenshaw, a Texas Republican who served as a Navy SEAL and was wounded in combat, said on Wednesday that he supported the Richard Star Act, but grew frustrated that the sleep apnea and tinnitus cuts were standing in the way of what he saw as important veterans package.Mr. Crenshaw did not vote on Mr. Takano’s bill on Thursday.

Mr. Crenshaw described the benefits for sleep apnea and tinnitus as “absurdly high” and said such assistance should have been changed long ago. He also criticized powerful veterans groups, specifically the Veterans of Foreign Wars, for lobbying lawmakers to oppose the Republican bill.

“Happy Veterans Day to everyone except the leadership of the V.F.W.” he said outside of the House chamber.

item.title: Polls Found Strength for Democrats, but Still Missed Badly
item.description:
In one important sense, polls got the story of this year’s election right: They showed Democrats winning the House and leading in the race for control of the Senate.

By another measure, this year’s polls were among the worst in recent memory. When looking across all pollsters, surveys systematically underestimated the support of Democratic candidates, and they did so on a scale that rivaled or even exceeded the heavily criticized misses of 2016 and 2020, when polls underestimated Republicans.

Overall, national polls this year underestimated the strength of Democrats by around four percentage points. Across the key Senate races, the polls underestimated Democrats by an even larger five-point miss, compared with an average of about 3.5 points across all Senate races.

Across the board, polls accurately called the winning party in each race while underestimating the Democratic margin.

New York Times analysis in select states where five or more polls were conducted in the final three weeks before Election Day. Excluding Alaska because results are not finalized.

The New York Times

This error is similar in size to the recent Trump-era polling presidential polling misfires. In 2020, national polls underestimated Republicans by about four percentage points; in 2016, Republicans were underestimated by three points.

Not every pollster this year erred by so much. The New York Times/Siena Poll, for instance, did not systematically underestimate the Democrats. Neither did a handful of other pollsters, including AtlasIntel and Survey 160.

Overall, the final Times/Siena polls underestimated Democrats by less than one percentage point, with some polls underestimating Democrats and others underestimating Republicans.

Note: In Nebraska, polling miss refers to over or underestimation of the independent, since there was no Democrat in the race.

Sources: New York Times/Siena polls of likely voters conducted Oct. 19 to 26 in Florida, South Carolina and Minnesota, Oct. 23 to 29 in Nebraska and Oct. 23 to Nov. 1 in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Michigan and Texas. Margins are calculated using candidates’ unrounded vote shares.

The New York Times

But across all pollsters, most polls underestimated Democrats, and in some states the error was huge. In Texas, the polls underestimated James Talarico’s margin of victory by nine percentage points. In general, the misses were less extreme in the classic northern battleground states, while pollsters struggled in the Sun Belt, where Democrats made their largest gains.

There are a number of theories as to why the error was so large. One particularly strong possibility is the role of turnout, which appears to have been far stronger for Democrats than many pollsters assumed.

The fact that the polling error has exceeded — or at least been on par with — the worst polling errors in recent history, however, suggests there may be something bigger and systematic at play.

Pollsters have adopted new sampling and weighting techniques to compensate for the voters they are failing to reach. More and more, pollsters are weighting their surveys to the respondents’ recalled vote history. But that approach assumes the composition of the electorate will look mostly the same from one cycle to the next, which this year led to polls being tilted toward Republicans.

When much of the industry responds to these challenges in the same ways, pollsters end up making similar mistakes. The kind of widespread polling error we’ve seen recently may become more common.

While the data isn’t final in much of the country, there are lots of signs that turnout was more favorable to the Democrats than most polls had anticipated.

Take Florida, for example. Unlike most other states, we already know the makeup of the Florida electorate: Registered Republicans outnumbered Democrats by about 8.5 percentage points, according to turnout information available from election officials. That’s not what most polls showed. Our final Times/Siena poll of the race, which overestimated Senator Ashley Moody’s support by three percentage points, had a likely electorate with Republicans ahead by 13 points in terms of party registration.

A similar story might have unfolded elsewhere in the South, where the Black and Hispanic share of the electorate was higher than it had been in previous cycles.

Why did the polls underestimate the Democratic turnout? The answer varies from pollster to pollster.

One factor might be that pollsters are relying on increasingly heavy-handed methods of weighting, where a pollster gives more weight to voters from groups who were underrepresented among survey respondents. Since 2016, and especially since 2020, pollsters have been trying to properly represent Mr. Trump’s supporters, in part by ensuring that they have the right number of people who reported voting for Mr. Trump in the previous election.

That approach may have overshot the mark this year. By weighting their samples to 2024 voting patterns, some pollsters may have assumed a more Republican electorate than the one that actually turned out.

(The Times/Siena Poll’s approach to incorporating the results of past elections is somewhat different than other public pollsters; read more here.)

New voters may have been an especially difficult group for pollsters to represent. Midterm elections tend to attract only the most regular voters, but Times Voter Trends estimates suggest that more than 10 percent of voters nationally didn’t vote in the last presidential election. Those voters backed Democrats by more than 30 points.

If a pollster missed the Democratic-friendly turnout and new voters, their results could be way off. An Emerson College poll in Texas, for example, underestimated Mr. Talarico’s win by 10 percentage points, and turnout was probably a factor. The poll found that voters who had backed Mr. Trump in 2024 outnumbered backers of Kamala Harris by 11 points; Times Voter Trends and exit poll data suggest that previous Trump voters outnumbered Harris voters by a much smaller margin, probably in the mid-single digits. The Emerson poll also found new voters making up just 3 percent of the electorate, compared to 15 percent of actual voters, according to Times Voter Trends.

Maine offers another potential instance of this, with polling from Marist finding Troy Jackson, the Democrat, ahead by nine percentage points among registered voters. The same poll, when accounting for the likeliest voters, had Mr. Jackson up by only two points. He won the state by six. With a different model of the electorate, Marist might have had a more accurate result.

Another possible source of error this year is that voters shifted over time, with Democrats seeming to gain strength, sometimes after surveys were no longer in the field.

Kansas provides a good example. A Times/Siena poll taken in September found the Senate race to be even. By October, another had Adam Hamilton ahead by five percentage points. In the end, he won the race by exactly that margin. Most other polls in the state followed a similar path.

This was the case across the Times/Siena polls this year when taken as a group.

Bars show how poll results in a given period differ from the eventual results.

Source: The New York Times/Siena 2026 Senate polls. The late-June polling wave covers Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas. The late-September wave includes Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. The late-October wave covers Florida, Minnesota, and South Carolina. Finally, the November results encompass Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nebraska, Ohio, and Texas. Nebraska is the only state in the analysis where the candidate was an independent rather than a Democrat.

The New York Times

Nationally, this was clear as well. A September Times/Siena poll had Democrats with a nine-percentage-point advantage in the race for the House, with that gap growing to 11 points by October. The final Times/Siena national poll was taken in mid-October, but other national polls showed Democrats’ strength continuing to grow in surveys taken in the final week before the election.

If other pollsters had been in the field closer to the election, it’s possible they would have gotten closer to the final result.

item.title: Anthony Clark, Comic and ‘Yes, Dear’ Star, Dies at 63
item.description:
Anthony Clark, a comedian and actor who is best known for his performance as Greg Warner on the sitcom “Yes, Dear,” died on Tuesday. He was 63.

His death was confirmed by his co-star on the show, Mike O’Malley, in a post on social media on Wednesday. He did not provide a cause of death.

“Yes, Dear” ran from 2000 to 2006 on CBS, in an era where multicamera sitcoms were still in vogue. The show followed two married couples navigating parenthood. Mr. Clark’s Greg was an uptight, first-time parent, contrasted with his more lax brother-in-law Jimmy, performed by Mr. O’Malley. The show was, in some ways, a commentary on overbearing parents overwhelmed by advice from professionals. TV reviewers were mostly tepid about “Yes, Dear,” but it drew steady ratings.

When Mr. Clark got the role, he was already an established stand-up comedian with sitcom experience. He was a regular on two short-lived series. One was “Boston Common” on NBC, where he portrayed Boyd Pritchett, a Virginia native who ends up working at his sister’s college. The other was “Soul Man,” a Dan Aykroyd vehicle where he played the Rev. Todd Tucker. Mr. Clark did not have to audition for the “Yes, Dear” role.

In a 2020 podcast interview with his longtime manager, Barry Katz, Mr. Clark described the process of shooting a sitcom as exhausting.

“It’s like taking a huge college campus test every Friday night when you shoot the show. You have to memorize 50 pages of script,” he said. “Let me tell you, if you don’t do it, there’s somebody on the next bus who will do it. So you better be good at it.”

Anthony Duane Clark was born on April 4, 1963, in Lynchburg, Va. His father, Charlie W. Clark Jr., was an assembly line worker for General Electric and his mother, Nellie R. Arrington, was a bookkeeper in a clothing store.

Mr. Clark wanted to leave small-town life, he told the Los Angeles Times in 1996. His performing career began at Emerson College in Boston, which counts Denis Leary and Jay Leno among its comedy alumni.

“I kind of realized that if I don’t get out of here I’m going to end up working a drive-through,” Mr. Clark said.

Arriving in Boston, he said, was like arriving in “Oz.” Within years, he was making a name for himself. He was in a student group that included one of his close friends, David Cross. His first time performing was at The Punchline, a comedy club in Atlanta.

“The reaction was incredible,” Mr. Clark told The Comic’s Comic, a blog, in 2006. “I was like, ‘Finally I get to be good at something.’”

Mr. Clark developed a reputation as a commanding performer with a Southern drawl. After graduating in 1987, he jumped to Hollywood quickly, which was unusual at the time for stand-up comedians. But the success of performers like Bill Cosby opened the door.

While he loved performing stand-up, acting was his true vocation. Mr. Clark credited Carol Burnett for making him want to be an actor in a 2001 New York Post interview.

Mr. Clark’s break came when he was referred by a former classmate from Emerson, who had become an assistant at the now-defunct Bresler-Kelly-Kipperman agency in New York.

“The agency picks up a client about every three years,” Mr. Clark told the Boston Globe in 1990. “So when they take on a new client everyone wants to know who he is immediately, so they’re all breaking down the door to meet me.”

One of his first roles came in “Dogfight,” the 1991 film starring River Phoenix. That was followed by a supporting role in “The Rock,” the 1996 film directed by Michael Bay, and guest appearances on “Ellen.”

But his life changed for good when he was cast in “Boston Common.”

“In my little life growing up in Virginia, I could have never imagined CBS,” Mr. Clark said on Mr. Katz’s podcast. “Come on. It’s the Carol Burnett network. You know what I mean?”

item.title: A Warrior Secretary and a Lesson at the Tomb of the Unknowns
item.description:
Pete Hegseth is possibly the most stage-managed secretary in the history of the Defense Department.

Almost everything he does, even his wardrobe choices, seems designed to either rally his supporters or provoke his critics. There are the American-flag pocket squares, the patriotic socks, the slicked-back hair, the “This is War” T-shirts and the carefully curated videos of him doing push-ups with the troops.

So many push-ups.

So it stood out when a soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknowns loudly scolded Mr. Hegseth and his party for laughing and talking near the solemn memorial on Veterans Day. Such interventions are a daily occurrence at Arlington Cemetery, where swarms of tourists brush up against strict military protocol.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the Army sentinel bellowed in the direction of Mr. Hegseth, his wife and his top advisers as they departed.

On Thursday, Mr. Hegseth awarded the soldier a Joint Service Commendation Medal. “We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth said on social media. “Carry on Patriots.”

The rare unscripted moment and its aftermath pointed to a larger truth about the military and its relationship to the country it serves.

An Iraq veteran and former Fox News host, Mr. Hegseth casts himself as the ultimate warrior and patriot, leading an elite force of like-minded souls. Today, only about one percent of Americans serve in the all-volunteer military, a fact often mentioned in Veterans Day speeches by presidents, politicians and Pentagon chiefs.

Most defense secretaries in recent decades have lamented the growing distance between soldiers and the nation they serve, citing it as a potential danger to the country’s democracy and the principle of civilian control of the military.

Mr. Hegseth, by contrast, appears to see the gap as proof of his and his troops’ moral and physical superiority.

“You are the real one percent,” he told hundreds of young officers and sergeants at his “State of the Force” speech in late September. “You feel comfortable inside the violence so that our citizens can live peacefully.”

Mr. Hegseth continued, pacing the stage in front of a giant American flag. The backdrop mirrored the portrayal of Gen. George S. Patton in the 1970 movie bearing his name.

“You don’t want to look like civilians, because you are different,” Mr. Hegseth told the troops. “You are set apart. You are warriors.”

Mr. Hegseth sounded a similar theme at a news conference on Tuesday in which he defended himself ahead of an impeachment vote in Congress. The defense secretary cast himself and the troops as targets of opportunistic politicians who would never understand their service.

He cited charges accusing him of carrying out unlawful strikes against suspected drug traffickers on boats in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific.

“Make no mistake about what is happening. This is not about me,” Mr. Hegseth said.

The true targets, he said, were the troops who had pulled the triggers.

“If they want to come for the warriors,” Mr. Hegseth vowed, “they’re going to have to come through me.”

Some senior military officers, who were granted anonymity to speak frankly about a superior, questioned Mr. Hegseth’s motives. Instead of taking responsibility for his orders, the defense secretary seemed to be hiding behind the troops, they said.

On Tuesday, the day before Veterans Day, Congress voted 211 to 204 to shelve the impeachment effort, shielding Mr. Hegseth from a damaging rebuke and a potential ouster.

In the aftermath of the vote, Mr. Hegseth and his team declared “TOTAL VICTORY!” in a message posted to social media.

“We will always stand tall and fight to defend the Republic!” wrote Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman.

The incident at Arlington Cemetery stood out as a rebuttal to this week’s unsuccessful impeachment effort and a reminder that the troops don’t belong to any single party, president or defense secretary, but rather to the nation they serve.

“Americans are lining up to serve in President Trump’s Department of War,” Mr. Hegseth declared on Tuesday at his news conference.

The statement caught the attention of Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling, a retired Army officer.

“It is not President Trump’s Department of War,” General Hertling said in a podcast episode. “It doesn’t belong to the president.”

item.title: Black Turnout Rose in Georgia, Powered by Younger Voters
item.description:
The Black share of the electorate in Georgia rose to its highest level in more than a decade, with the turnout rate among young Black voters outpacing that of young white voters. Both trends contributed to a heavy leftward shift in the state this year.

Democrats had a historically good election night in Georgia. Senator Jon Ossoff won re-election by 18 percentage points, which was the largest margin of victory for a statewide Democrat in more than two decades. Down the ballot, the party romped to victory, flipping the state house and every statewide office. That included the governorship, with Keisha Lance Bottoms elected the first Black governor in Georgia’s history.

Black voter enthusiasm, particularly in the South, was closely watched in the midterm elections after a Supreme Court ruling in April that weakened the Voting Rights Act, setting off a wave of redistricting that diluted Black representation in several states.

Georgia is one of the first states to report its validated voter history for 2026, which is a record of exactly who voted in the election. It is also one of only a handful of states where voters can provide their race when they register to vote.

The result is a glimpse at Black voters’ role in elections that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, albeit from one state.

Turnout was crucial. Based on voter data taken directly from the state, Black voters made up at least 30 percent of Georgia’s electorate in 2026, the highest of any election since 2012, when President Barack Obama ran for re-election. The true share is likely to be slightly higher — around 7 percent of voters in Georgia’s voter file are listed as “other” or “unknown” for race. Times Voter Trends, which models the race of these voters, estimates the Black share of this year’s electorate at around 32 percent.

Because Black voters in Georgia are overwhelmingly Democratic — more than 95 percent of them voted for Mr. Ossoff this year, according to Times Voter Trends — even small increases in the Black share of the electorate can translate to sizable gains for the party.

For the first time since 2012, turnout rates among Black voters under 30 were slightly higher than those of white voters under 30.

Source: Georgia Secretary of State. Turnout rates by race and age are based on Georgia’s voter history files joined to the state’s contemporaneous voter files, as a share of registered voters. They do not include voters whose race is classified as “other” or “unknown.”

The New York Times

Much of the surge in Democratic support in Georgia was fueled by voters under 30, across all racial groups. Their swing toward Democrats was more than twice as large as Georgia voters’ as a whole. Like young voters in other states, this group shifted modestly toward Donald Trump in 2024 before lurching back to the left this time.

Turnout tends to decline in midterm elections, particularly among younger voters, but higher turnout among young white voters has been the recent norm in midterm and presidential years.

In 2022, 33 percent of registered white voters under 30 cast a ballot, compared with 22 percent of registered Black voters under 30 — a gap that was virtually erased in the 2026 election.

item.title: Kalshi Severs Its Relationship With Donald Trump Jr.
item.description:
Kalshi, the nation’s leading prediction market, said on Thursday that Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, would no longer serve as an adviser.

The firm’s officials said in a statement that they and Donald Trump Jr. had agreed to part ways because his investment firm, 1789, had heavily invested in Polymarket, Kalshi’s biggest competitor. A spokesman for Donald Trump Jr. confirmed that the decision was mutual.

It was not immediately clear whether the president’s oldest son would keep the shares in Kalshi given to him as part of his compensation package when it hired him in January 2025. Those assets are now estimated to be worth millions.

Kalshi said it reached out to Donald Trump Jr. this fall to discuss ending his contract after 1789, in August, added about $300 million to its investments in Polymarket on top of its earlier contributions of about $200 million.

“Both parties understood that advising two competitors in a growing sector was complicating things,” the company said in a statement. Kalshi’s decision was reported earlier Thursday by Reuters.

The Trump administration has been a huge booster of prediction markets. After sweeping the midterm elections, Democrats in Congress have promised to investigate allegations of self-dealing by the administration. Some critics have pointed to federal regulatory approvals given to Kalshi as a prime example of the administration’s conflicts of interest.

Most recently, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets, authorized Kalshi to offer a type of trading on stocks, cryptocurrencies and other assets without owning them, which had not been allowed before in the United States. Those decisions, starting in May, prompted highly unusual lawsuits from major trading clearinghouses, claiming that the C.F.T.C. was violating federal laws designed to protect investors and financial markets.

The administration has also taken on both red and blue states that claim Kalshi and other prediction markets are subject to state regulations and laws governing sports betting. The C.F.T.C. has taken the opposite view, backing Kalshi in a slew of lawsuits with the states. Donald Trump Jr. echoed the C.F.T.C.’s stance in a closed-door meeting with Republican state attorneys general in March.

Through his spokesman, the president’s son has previously said he was involved only in helping Kalshi market itself, not in negotiating with the federal government.

item.title: Republican Setbacks Swell in the South With Stinging Loss in Mississippi
item.description:
Republicans were routed in Georgia and stunned in South Carolina. In Louisiana, a Republican Senate candidate won by less than two percentage points against a little-known Democrat who ran just two TV commercials.

Then came Wednesday in Mississippi, where Scott Colom became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in 44 years, defeating Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and further shaking Republicans’ once-unquestioned hold on the South.

Now, after the series of midterm shocks, Southern Republicans have been left to confront a new reality: A region they dominated for years is no longer a lock for their party.

“Republicans fell asleep at the wheel,” said Bill Armistead, a former chair of the Alabama Republican Party, adding, “If we stay asleep at the wheel, we could see some losses in the future.”

Republicans also lost their grip on the Georgia governor’s mansion, suffered a staggering loss by nearly 20 points in North Carolina’s Senate race and surrendered seats in state houses in Tennessee, Alabama and Arkansas. In South Carolina, 10 state legislative seats flipped into Democratic hands.

Some Southern Republicans said their party’s midterm performance was a historical outlier in a year when Democrats made sweeping gains across the country with campaigns that capitalized on anger with inflation and President Trump. Democrats, who continue to face brand and image problems, could face difficulties keeping their gains in the South in future elections held in less favorable political climates.

At the same time, other Republicans begrudgingly believe that the South’s political trajectory is shifting under their feet. And Democrats have signaled that they plan to keep their focus on the South, with their 2028 presidential nominating process starting in South Carolina.

The unsettling midterm performance for Southern Republicans comes at a moment of uncertainty for their party, as Mr. Trump enters the lame-duck stage of his second term, the coalitions he has built fracture, and college-educated voters appear to be flocking to Democrats. Republicans are also reckoning with lost ground among Black voters, who make up a significant share of the electorate in the South and were angered by G.O.P. efforts to redraw congressional districts in ways that diluted their influence.

“I hope this is a wake-up call for all of my Republican colleagues,” said Mike Hurst, the chairman of the Mississippi Republican Party. He added that Republicans could not take the state’s governor’s race next year for granted. “I think it will be competitive, and I think we as Republicans will have to work to earn the trust of the voters.”

Mr. Colom’s defeat of Ms. Hyde-Smith, who had held her seat since 2018, sent particular reverberations across the South, given how widely Mississippi had been viewed as a hub of loyal conservatives. Mr. Colom made history with his win, becoming the first Black senator in the state since the 1800s.

Black voters, who make up about 40 percent of Mississippi’s population, the largest share of any state, largely back Democrats and have repeatedly elected the state’s lone House Democrat, Representative Bennie Thompson. White voters in the state have long voted for Republicans in huge numbers.

The Senate result in Mississippi suggested that the racial polarization that has helped propel Republican candidates in the South for decades is weakening, said Brian Robinson, a Republican strategist in Georgia.

Mr. Colom was lifted by his remarkable strength in the Memphis suburbs in northwestern Mississippi. In DeSoto County, a majority-white county made up of Memphis suburbs that Mr. Trump won by 24 points in 2024, Mr. Colom beat Ms. Hyde-Smith by about eight points.

White voters with college degrees, who decades ago were safely Republican, have been gravitating toward Democrats, Mr. Robinson said.

“That’s changed forever,” Mr. Robinson said, expressing uneasiness about Republicans’ standing in his home state of Georgia. “I do think for an extended period of time North Carolina and Mississippi are going to be competitive. I hope Georgia can be competitive.”

In Georgia, the Republican Senate nominee, Representative Mike Collins, lost to the Democratic incumbent, Senator Jon Ossoff, by about 18 percentage points. The Democratic candidate for governor, former Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms of Atlanta, also won comfortably to become the first Black person elected the state’s governor and the first Black woman elected governor anywhere in the United States.

In Mississippi, Mr. Hurst, the Republican Party chairman, acknowledged the “incredible milestone” of Mr. Colom becoming that state’s first Black senator in nearly 150 years.

Mr. Colom was lifted by his remarkable strength in the Memphis suburbs in northwestern Mississippi. In DeSoto County, a majority-white county made up of Memphis suburbs that Mr. Trump won by 24 points in 2024, Mr. Colom beat Ms. Hyde-Smith by about eight points.

Republicans will face another test in Mississippi next year when they try to defend the seat of Gov. Tate Reeves, who is term-limited.

They must now confront a triumphant base of Democratic voters, as well as questions about whether the coalition of Black voters, white liberals and disaffected conservatives that Mr. Colom harnessed this year will remain cohesive.

Part of that likely depends on how Mr. Colom carves his path as part of the new generation of Southern Democrats arriving to power in Washington and state capitols.

“I’m going to treat your future the way I want my future to be,” Mr. Colom said in his victory speech on Wednesday. “My commitment is to be someone that continues to stay in prayer, continues to have faith and continues to work to make every Mississippian’s life better.”

There is also an open question about whether Mississippi Republicans will move to redraw district lines in the coming weeks after the Supreme Court this year weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Lawmakers held a series of public hearings before the November elections, but they have not said whether they will make changes or how if they do.

The Supreme Court decision, as well as the ensuing scramble to undercut majority-Black districts across the South, helped galvanize Black voters in Mississippi to support Mr. Colom. It also helped pushed voters across the region to turn out for Democrats in the midterms.

Some Mississippi Republicans said the outcome in the state’s Senate race was still more a reflection of a broader frustration with high prices, the Trump administration’s tariffs and the economic toll of the Iran war.

“Let’s put it in perspective: This is one statewide race,” said State Senator Scott DeLano, a Republican, noting that all three of Mississippi’s Republican congressmen comfortably won re-election. “I don’t think that this is a foretelling of things to come in Mississippi.”

Hs said it was clear that Republicans in Mississippi were making a statement against the war and high food and gasoline prices, and that Mr. Colom’s campaign had taken advantage.

State Senator Michael McLendon, a Republican, agreed that Ms. Hyde-Smith had been “absolutely” outworked by Mr. Colom, and that Mr. Colom’s message carried greater potency at a time when voters were exasperated with high prices.

“It was a perfect storm,” Mr. McLendon said.

But he also said the election offered a lesson to Mississippi Republicans.

“You better not take any races for granted,” he said. “It’s a different climate.”

item.title: Democrats Hold Kansas Governorship, Retaining Power on the Plains
item.description:
State Senator Cindy Holscher won election as governor of Kansas, keeping the seat in Democratic hands for a third straight term, The Associated Press said on Thursday.

She narrowly defeated Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee and the president of the Kansas Senate. Gov. Laura Kelly, the Democratic incumbent, was barred by term limits from seeking re-election.

Ms. Holscher’s victory added to a momentous election for Democrats in Kansas and across the country, and it maintained a rare lever of power for the party on the Great Plains.

Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, became the first Kansas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race since the 1930s. In addition, Democrats flipped several legislative seats to break a Republican supermajority in the Kansas House of Representatives, which will make it much harder to override vetoes by Ms. Holscher.

Kansans also voted out Attorney General Kris W. Kobach, a Republican who helped elevate illegal voting as a political issue. Republicans prevailed in other statewide races and will still have majorities in both legislative chambers.

Though Kansans reliably vote for Republicans for president, they have shown an independent streak in midterm elections, swinging for decades between Republican and Democratic governors. High costs, dissatisfaction with President Trump’s policies and a tangle of challenges facing farmers made the Plains region more winnable for Democrats this year.

Both parties spent heavily on the race for Kansas governor. For Republicans, it represented a tantalizing flip opportunity on an otherwise foreboding electoral map. For Democrats, it was a chance to maintain power in a reliably conservative state.

Ms. Holscher, a lawmaker from suburban Kansas City, ran on a populist platform that called for legalizing marijuana and placing a moratorium on data centers. She also promised to prioritize funding for public schools and to reduce property taxes. She will be the fourth woman to serve as governor of Kansas.

“I stand with the people — not the corporations, not the billionaires,” Ms. Holscher said in a debate at the State Fair.

Ms. Holscher emerged from a competitive Democratic primary in which Governor Kelly had endorsed a different candidate. Ms. Kelly had also publicly questioned Ms. Holscher’s ability to win a general election, suggesting that the candidate had positioned herself too far to the left. After the primary, Ms. Kelly endorsed Ms. Holscher.

Ms. Kelly said in a post-election interview that she was “more confident now that Cindy will be a good governor.”

“You really have to look at things very differently when you’re governing than you do when you’re campaigning,” Ms. Kelly said, “and I am absolutely confident that Cindy Holscher will surround herself with good people, and that she’ll keep things moving forward.”

Ms. Holscher will be the first Democratic governor elected to succeed a fellow Democrat in Kansas history. Her running mate, State Representative KC Ohaebosim, is the first Black person to win statewide office in Kansas since the 1880s.

Mr. Masterson, a legislator from the Wichita area, emphasized his endorsement from Mr. Trump on the campaign trail. He pledged to lower taxes and cut costs for residents.

In a statement on Thursday, Mr. Masterson said it “looks like we will come up just short” and that he had called Ms. Holscher to congratulate her.

“This was a hard election for people who share our vision, here and across the country,” Mr. Masterson added.

Though not a household name in much of the state, Mr. Masterson amassed considerable power at the Kansas Capitol. During his tenure as president of the State Senate, lawmakers overrode Ms. Kelly’s vetoes to enact dozens of bills, including ones that placed restrictions on transgender people, overhauled election procedures and limited officials’ ability to impose restrictions during public health emergencies.

But with Ms. Kelly in office, Mr. Masterson’s power was sometimes limited. Though he and other legislative Republicans wanted to redraw the state’s congressional map last year, he would have needed near-unanimous Republican support to overcome a veto from the governor. That plan unraveled when several Republicans voiced opposition, leaving in place a single Democratic-leaning U.S. House district.

item.title: Rescue Ends in Brooklyn After 8 Die in Building Collapse
item.description:
After a night of frantic searches through the rubble of a Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people, New York City officials announced on Thursday that they were ending their rescue efforts, concluding there were no more victims.

Eighteen other people, including four firefighters, were injured in the collapse and its aftermath at 1321 Flatbush Avenue. Two children who were cousins were among the eight killed, according to an internal police report. Three were construction workers.

The tragedy shattered the heavily immigrant neighborhood and set off a city investigation into excavation at the construction site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue.

The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. on Wednesday. James Williams, who works at a deli across the street, said he had been hearing an incessant loud hammering noise every few minutes from the construction site on Wednesday afternoon. He went outside and saw bricks falling from 1321 Flatbush, a three-story apartment building. “I’m like, Oh hell, what is going on?” he said.

He watched as the building started to crumble, its front and side sliding away, and a check-cashing shop that he frequented underneath all collapsing into the open construction site next door. He saw clothes and a microwave oven thrown into the dust-filled air. He heard people scream.

The first firefighters arrived within a minute, followed by more from around New York City and from New Rochelle, N.Y., in Westchester County. The search and rescue efforts involved about 250 personnel in all.

At 2625 Bedford, city officials had approved plans for a three-story building, and the developers of the site had submitted paperwork for a nine-story building with 64 apartments, a community space and a grocery store. Previously, it had been home to a one-story building.

City officials said that the developers had an active permit for excavation and foundation work on the lot and that workers were excavating at the time of the collapse. Photos of the site showed shoring holding up the walls of the excavation site.

In March, the New York City Department of Buildings had ordered the property owner to stop demolition work at the site after it found that there was inadequate protection for nearby properties. The department lifted the order in August after finding that the project team had corrected the violations.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who pledged “a full and thorough” investigation into the collapse, said that officials had identified five entities associated with the construction site and were “commencing sweeps” of roughly 100 other sites across the city that had ties to them.

Mr. Mamdani said that he was “incredibly troubled” that construction had continued at the site even though an inspection report in March had identified cracks in the north facade of the collapsed building. He said the city would hold anyone responsible for unsafe conditions “fully accountable.”

“This has been a devastating evening and morning for our city,” the mayor said. “We are mourning too many people who we love.”

The general contractor at the construction site, Townhouse Builders, and the engineer on the project, LMW Engineering Group, did not respond to requests for comment. The limited liability company that owns the property is associated with two women, Faigy Fischman and Judy Swimer. A man who answered a phone number listed for Ms. Fischman declined to speak to a reporter. Ms. Swimer did not respond to a message left at a phone number listed under her name.

The collapsed building, which had faded letters on the facade that read “Ceasar Building,” was built in 1930 and had four apartments, with a commercial space on the ground floor, according to city records. It was the last in a row of 10 nearly identical buildings, and sat on a block with a corner deli, a furniture store, a nail salon, a pharmacy, a Pentecostal church and a day care center. The dead, Mr. Mamdani said, included parents and children, “young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad and beyond.”

As rain started to pelt Brooklyn on Thursday, rescue workers were still scouring the site with search dogs, drones, helicopters, fire trucks and heavy machinery. The collapse sheared off the wall of an adjacent building, leaving a staircase, a pink bedroom and closets filled with clothing exposed to the elements.

The American Red Cross said 14 adults and five children in seven households had signed up for emergency assistance, including temporary housing.

The police identified the eight victims as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Barry Mamadou, 23; Edgar Sapón, 26; José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26; Ndiaye Mamadou, 31; and Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31.

Mr. Siguencia migrated from Ecuador in March 2025 and started working on the construction site two weeks ago, according to his mother, Leanor Yupa. She had watched as rescue crews hauled debris out of the site. When she learned that her son was among the dead, she dropped to her knees and screamed.

A family friend, Javier Ortega, said that Mr. Siguencia “came here looking for a better life, a means to live, like so many migrants do.”

Mr. Sapón, who was also a construction worker at the site, came to the United States from Guatemala three years ago. His relatives had spent the night searching for him at the morgue and then watching as bodies were pulled from the rubble, said Marisela Vasquez, 35, whose niece was married to Mr. Sapón. He had a 6-year-old son, and his wife arrived Wednesday evening after hearing of the collapse, hoping to find him.

Mr. Caguana Cosquillo, an immigrant from Ecuador and also a construction worker at the site, was supporting a growing family. He would pick up his 4-year-old son at a nursery school in Bushwick, Brooklyn, said Alexandra Simonian, the son’s teacher, and his wife is expecting a child this month. “They were very attached, a very sweet kind of family,” she said.

After the collapse on Wednesday, more than a dozen firefighters pulled a pregnant woman from the rubble, as her husband broke down in tears. “She is still alive,” the man said at an impromptu news conference near the scene. “I am very happy.”

Farah Louis, a City Council member who represents the neighborhood, said on Thursday that the woman, who was from the West African nation of Guinea, was in stable condition at a hospital.

“This is a very close-knit community,” Ms. Louis said, adding, “These folks are our neighbors. They’re our friends. That’s why the community is so heartbroken.”

The collapse renewed concerns about the rapid development that has been transforming Brooklyn. Carlo A. Scissura, the president of the New York Building Congress, a construction and real estate trade group, said smaller projects outside Midtown Manhattan often do not get the same close scrutiny, a frustration that many residents share.

“I know a lot of people are not a fan of the new construction,” said Yolanda Solomon, a pastor in Flatbush. “It seems it happened so fast.”

Reporting was contributed by Liam Stack, Emma G. Fitzsimmons, Sharon Otterman, Caitlyn Freeman, Chelsia Rose Marcius, Maria Cramer, Mihir Zaveri, Todd Heisler, Christopher Maag, Andy Newman, Kaja Andric and Wesley Parnell.

item.title: What Does 2026 Mean for the Map in 2028?
item.description:
America’s political map looked pretty calcified — until last week.

Democrats’ surprising midterm wins across red states — including Scott Colom’s victory over Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi — have raised new questions for both parties that will matter a lot for 2028 and beyond.

Was this all a blip, specific to this particular moment? Or could America’s political map be changing in a bigger way, putting longtime Republican strongholds in play for Democrats?

Tonight, let’s dive into the biggest question coming out of the midterms.

Since 2016, just six states have actually swung between Democratic and Republican presidential candidates. In the Senate, red-state Democrats and blue-state Republicans became endangered species. And the map of competitive House districts grew ever narrower.

But Democrats’ big Senate flips last week mostly came in states that haven’t backed their party for president in years.

“When you start losing Mississippi and Maine simultaneously, then you clearly have lost popular sentiment,” Newt Gingrich, the former House speaker, told me.

He would know. In 1994, he led his party to make enormous gains in the House, a “Republican revolution” that set the stage for the map we know today. And he believes that Democrats’ wins last week just might be the beginning of a rare political realignment, depending on how they govern.

“If the Democrats can discipline themselves to listen to the American people, they could create a new majority that could govern for quite a long time,” he said.

There is no guarantee, of course, that any wave election will become more than a one-off. In 1946, the year after Franklin D. Roosevelt’s death and Harry Truman’s ascent, Republicans swept Democrats out of the House and Senate — only to see their power ebb again two years later when Truman, a Democrat, won a full term.

And in 2006, Democrats captured both the House and the Senate as the public tired of George W. Bush, then deepened their control of government with the 2008 rise of President Barack Obama. Then, of course, came the “shellacking” of 2010, when Republicans picked up seats in the Senate and gained control of the House.

But sometimes, a wave election can signal the start of something more long-term.

Take 1964, when Lyndon B. Johnson, Democrat, won 44 states and Washington, D.C. It was a Democratic landslide. But a band of states in the Deep South backed Barry Goldwater, that year’s Republican presidential nominee, and those states have mostly stuck with Republicans ever since, especially when it comes to presidential elections.

And look at the presidential map in 1996. Two years after Gingrich first won power in the House, you can see the last gasps of Democratic dominance in Southern states like West Virginia, Arkansas and Tennessee — states that became seemingly impossible for the party to win when President Bill Clinton was no longer on the ballot.

Democrats believe they now have the opportunity to reimagine their party’s path to power, which in recent presidential elections has run through the “blue wall” states of Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. A party that can compete in the South — or even just in Texas, which has 40 electoral votes — has a lot more ways to win.

I called Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, who believes that this is the moment for Democrats to go all in on winning in Southern states, which have not in recent years been seen as critical to what he called “the math of our majority.” Now, he said, they should be.

“The South is the fastest-growing region in the country,” Warnock said. “It’s the only region in the country where we’re seeing population growth for every age group. And when you look at the base of the Democratic Party and its most loyal voters, Black voters, the South is where the big and valiant struggle for our voices is being waged.”

Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky told me he thought red states that just elected Democratic governors, like Ohio and Iowa, could remain competitive in 2028.

“Democrats were looking in ’28 and ’32 at a shrinking map with very little margin of error,” he said. “Now they’re going to be able to go and campaign in states, lean on Democratic governors that have won in those states, and know how to turn out voters.”

It’s much too early to know what the 2028 map is going to look like. But the uncertainty about the nation’s political geography is new, and could shape the contest in unpredictable ways.

quote of the day

That was Hunter Patterson, a police dispatcher in Montgomery County, Texas. A “libertarian independent,” he said he usually voted Republican but no longer considered himself one after the party’s sharp turn to the right in recent years.

Patterson said he disagreed with James Talarico on many things, but still voted for him for Senate.

The question of what independent-minded voters like Patterson do in the future will go a long way to determining whether states like Texas snap back to red, or stay purple.

My colleague Sabrina Tavernise spoke with lots of them. Read her reporting.

CATCH ME UP

Jensen Huang, the embattled chief executive of the chip giant Nvidia, resigned, sending shock waves through the tech industry.

His downfall costs the A.I. boom one of its top backers, Ben Casselman writes.

Trump said that he would pull back Vice President JD Vance from potential peace talks with Iran, and that Vance’s time would be better spent focused on domestic fraud.

Will Democrats fight to impeach or investigate Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. with their new majorities? Or, Sheryl Gay Stolberg writes, will they try to work with him on areas where they can agree?

House Democrats faced a backlash after 11 of them missed a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Hospitals across the country are racing to keep millions of patients insured, and bracing for huge funding cuts, before new Medicaid work rules and guidelines begin in the new year.

Cities are employing a new strategy to delay the Trump administration’s effort to build ICE jails: using a lawsuit to stall the construction of immigration detention centers until Democrats take over Congress.

q+A

One Senate race has yet to be called: Alaska’s.

Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, is narrowly leading Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and an analysis of ballots by The New York Times found that she is likely to prevail. But the state’s ranked-choice voting system means that tallying votes there is extra complicated.

My colleague Christine Zhang, a reporter on our Election Analytics team, has been watching the count closely, and is here with a quick update.

Christine, what’s happening in Alaska right now? Why is their count taking so long?

Alaska has reported 86 percent of the votes so far. The remaining ballots are mostly mail-in ballots, which need to be reviewed before being included in the count. It can also take a long time to transport mail ballots through the state’s remote, inaccessible regions. Officials will count ballots that arrive up to 10 days after Election Day, as long as they were postmarked by Nov. 3.

How much longer do officials there have to count?

They have until Nov. 18 to count all the remaining ballots. That’s also the date when ranked-choice tabulation will begin if the top candidates in the statewide races have not cleared the 50 percent threshold needed to win outright.

During this process, whoever is in last place will be eliminated, and the votes for that candidate will instead be awarded to each voter’s next choice still in the race. That goes on until two candidates are left, and the one with more votes wins.

OK. Is Nov. 18 when we might officially learn the winner of the race?

Well, there’s a chance that the Senate race could be called sooner, if it doesn’t go to ranked-choice tabulation at all. The remaining vote is from areas favorable to Peltola, so we’ll have to see how it goes in the days ahead. But yes, if the race is decided by ranked-choice tabulation, we will most likely know on Nov. 18.

in the states

In 2024, voters in states like Arizona and Missouri backed abortion-rights measures even as they supported candidates like President Trump who had celebrated the fall of Roe v. Wade.

This year, the reverse has happened. As Democratic candidates won statewide races, several high-profile conservative ballot measures prevailed. The dissonant results show that voters do not always move the same way all at once — even in a wave election.

California narrowly killed a measure for a wealth tax on billionaires.

Arizona handily passed a Republican-backed referendum to require transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms aligned with the sex listed on their birth certificates. Voters in three more states, including Colorado, passed similar measures.

Voters in seven states, including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio, passed measures to ban noncitizen voting or require voter identification — ideas long pushed by conservative groups.

Two more Republican bright spots:

New England’s two Republican governors withstood the blue wave. Read about how they did it.

Paul LePage, the former governor of Maine, flipped a House seat in a rare midterm battleground win for Republicans.

ONE LAST THING

Bruce Giudici tried for years to win a seat on the board of supervisors in Calaveras County, Calif. Then he died. But his odds of winning the seat are looking better than ever.

On Aug. 30, his campaign said, he was out door-knocking when he fell. Giudici, who was 68, died the next day. His campaign pushed forward anyway, and its grass-roots politicking seems to have paid off: Giudici has posthumously received 57 percent of the vote in his race.

Taylor Robinson and Christine Zhang contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Had Urged Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to Fight for His Job
item.description:
President Trump called Jensen Huang on Tuesday, before the Nvidia chief stepped down amid a rapidly unfolding spy scandal, and urged him to keep fighting for his job, according to two people briefed on the conversation.

The call was the latest instance of Mr. Trump defending and protecting Mr. Huang, who had become a high-profile ally and an influential adviser on artificial intelligence. The president continued to back him to the end, even after U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia announced on Thursday that Mr. Huang, who built the company into the world’s leading supplier of advanced A.I. chips, had been replaced as chief executive following revelations not just of the affair with the woman suspected of being a spy, but also another with one of his employees.

A representative for Mr. Huang did not provide a comment for this article. Neither Mr. Trump nor the White House responded to requests for comment about his call to Mr. Huang.

The president had been warned at least twice about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a Chinese citizen known as Alice Huang, whom intelligence agencies concluded had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, The New York Times has reported. The first warning was late last year, and the second was in the spring.

Mr. Trump took no action either time, and brought Mr. Huang with him on a trip to China in May. In recent days, he has publicly praised Mr. Huang and expressed sympathy for him, saying in a social media post on Thursday that he was a “legend.”

The president’s advisers said he was blasé about the national security implications when told of the intelligence community assessments related to Mr. Huang. One aide said that Mr. Trump saw the episode mainly through the lens of adultery, and that the president dismissed the idea of Mr. Huang’s entanglement posing a threat to the country.

Mr. Trump saw Nvidia as essentially too big to fail, aides said. The company, one of the world’s largest by market capitalization, has played a vital role in the global economy and underpinned the president’s hopes for A.I. dominance over China.

Advisers to Mr. Trump gave several explanations for the way he had handled the matter, speaking on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive conversations.

Chief among them was that the president had invested greatly in Mr. Huang, whom he saw as a modern-day Henry Ford, leading in a technology that could define the century.

Mr. Trump viewed Nvidia’s fortunes as bound up with those of the U.S. economy and the stock market. When reports surfaced that the company’s board was considering removing Mr. Huang, Mr. Trump asked confidants what they thought would happen to the markets. He was worried that Mr. Huang’s ouster could cause a sharp downturn.

The president’s last-ditch effort to save Mr. Huang was a remarkable moment in a relationship that barely existed two years ago.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Huang was nowhere on his radar. The Nvidia founder had no real presence in Washington. He did not lobby or give to campaigns, and showed little interest in politics. The Biden administration’s sweeping restrictions on chip exports forced Mr. Huang to be more attentive to Washington, but he still did far less politicking than his rivals. In contrast to other tech leaders, he did not attend Mr. Trump’s second inauguration.

With evident relish, Mr. Trump has told the story of first hearing Mr. Huang’s name. “Who the hell is he? What’s his name?” he has recalled to associates. “His name is Jensen Huang of Nvidia. I said, ‘What the hell is Nvidia?’”

By late 2024, Mr. Trump had learned that Mr. Huang was the indispensable man at the company that controlled at least 80 percent of the market for chips used to train the most advanced A.I. models. And Mr. Huang saw an opening to woo a president who demanded personal attention and responded to flattery.

In April 2025, Mr. Huang and his wife, Lori, attended a dinner at Mar-a-Lago with Mr. Trump and a group of tech and crypto donors. The president came away intrigued, and the more he learned, the more impressed he became, people who spoke with him at the time said. He was told again and again that the A.I. boom ran almost entirely through Nvidia. “You’re taking over the world, Jensen,” Mr. Trump would later tell him.

Mr. Huang offered something the president had failed to get in his first term and hoped to achieve in his second. During his first administration, Mr. Trump had pledged to bring back coal and steel jobs. But those industries never returned to their old strength.

In a second term, A.I. offered another route to the reindustrialization of the United States that Mr. Trump had promised voters. He came to believe that the rush to build data centers, and their enormous appetite for electricity, could produce a manufacturing revival and keep an otherwise shaky economy running hot, people close to him said. To the president, that made the leaders of the A.I. companies the most valuable executives in the country, and Mr. Huang perhaps the most valuable of them all.

Mr. Huang played into that savior role. In 2025, he said Nvidia would produce up to $500 billion of A.I. infrastructure in the United States. He also praised the president lavishly.

“America’s unique advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump,” he said that July. He traveled with Mr. Trump to the Persian Gulf in May 2025, where the president announced deals for Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates to buy Nvidia chips. He provided the kind of deal-making headlines that Mr. Trump craved.

Mr. Huang had persuaded Mr. Trump that Nvidia should sell its chips as widely as possible, so that the world would build on U.S., rather than Chinese, technology. David Sacks, the White House’s A.I. and crypto czar, backed him. The two men helped persuade Mr. Trump to plant himself on the unpopular side of a major issue for the populist right.

China hawks on the MAGA right, including Stephen K. Bannon, wanted chip sales to China banned outright. But Mr. Trump sided with Mr. Huang and his billionaire counterparts leading other tech companies, including OpenAI, Meta and SpaceX.

At Mr. Huang’s urging, Mr. Trump allowed Nvidia to sell certain models of its chips to China under an unusual arrangement in which the federal government took 15 percent, and later 25 percent, of the revenue. Critics raised legal questions and warned that national security was being sold out. Administration officials privately marveled at how much sway Mr. Huang seemed to have with the president.

Some U.S. officials had worried about Mr. Huang long before the spy scandal broke into the open this fall. They saw him as, at best, naïve and careless in his dealings with Chinese executives and local officials, with whom he kept close ties. Some wondered how he could possibly have been oblivious to Ms. Huang’s possible connections to Chinese intelligence.

But Mr. Trump was never likely to share in those national security concerns. While he has used bellicose campaign rhetoric against China — he has accused Beijing of “raping” the American economy and made that line of attack a focus of his 2016 presidential campaign — he has never been a China hawk in any conventional sense.

Throughout the president’s terms, his aggressive posture on China has been limited to trade. And even there he has repeatedly shown he would rather cut a deal with Xi Jinping, the country’s leader, than engage in a protracted trade war.

Unlike some of his predecessors, Mr. Trump has largely ignored Beijing’s human rights abuses. Asked in 2020 why he had not imposed sanctions over the mass detention of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, he said, “Well, we were in the middle of a major trade deal.”

People close to the president say that in private, he has questioned why the United States would ever go to war over Taiwan.

To dramatize his disregard for the small island nation, Mr. Trump has been known to hold up a teaspoon to lunch guests at his golf club and say, “This is Taiwan.”

item.title: Van Hollen Says He Will Challenge Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
item.description:
Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced on Thursday that he would challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for majority leader, setting up a clash among Democrats just as they were celebrating their new majority and planning for a takeover of Congress in January.

The move by Mr. Van Hollen, a progressive Democrat elected to the Senate in 2016 after seven terms in the House representing the Washington, D.C. suburbs, comes as some Democratic senators and activists have called for an alternative to Mr. Schumer, a moderate whom they regard as too tied to the party establishment to lead a newly energized party forward in the next Congress.

Mr. Van Hollen, who is also said to be weighing a run for president in 2028, had emerged as the favorite to challenge Mr. Schumer for the post and had expressed increasing willingness to do so in recent days.

Senate Democrats are scheduled to vote behind closed doors on Dec. 1 to determine who will be their leader when their party takes the Senate majority on Jan. 4.

“I think there is a big appetite for change within the Democratic Caucus,” Mr. Van Hollen said in an interview before the announcement. “I think people want to have a system of much more meaningful input, and that’s going to be even more important now that we have this large majority.”

His announcement came as Mr. Schumer and his allies reiterated that the New York Democrat had commitments of support from well over the majority of Senate Democrats needed to re-elect him as leader.

In a statement, Mr. Schumer said that he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead.”

“I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader,” he said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

Mr. Schumer oversaw the Senate Democratic campaign effort that has flipped at least eight Senate seats, with the Democrat Scott Colom on Wednesday called as the winner in the Mississippi Senate race. The Alaska Senate race result has not been called, but the Democrat Mary Peltola is slightly ahead there.

Despite that success, some in the ranks of Senate Democrats have called for a broad discussion of party leadership going forward and a debate over the agenda the party should pursue.

Other Democrats say that the leadership fight is distracting from the stunning victory Democrats recorded on Nov. 3 and hurting their preparation for January.

“We were at 47-53 and now we are at 55, 56,” said Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania and a strong supporter of Mr. Schumer. He added: “I don’t understand why that’s a conversation.”

Other Democrats have noted the contrast of Senate Republicans returning their leadership team without a challenge after losing at least 8 seats while Democrats are embroiled in a showdown despite their win.

Mr. Van Hollen, 67, is the child of a diplomat and was elected to the House in 2002 after entering the race as an underdog in a very competitive primary while serving in the Maryland legislature.

In the House, he became a close ally to Speaker Nancy Pelosi and a leading voice on budget issues. In 2008, he led the House campaign effort as Democrats expanded their majority when Barack Obama was elected president and also led the campaign team in 2010.

Mr. Van Hollen was seen as a potential future speaker in the House, but that prospect seemed far-off given Ms. Pelosi’s hold on the office. When Barbara Mikulski of Baltimore was set to retire from the Senate in 2016, he sought her seat and won. Given his experience, Senate Democrats immediately put him in charge of their campaign organization.

In the Senate, Mr. Van Hollen has focused on budget issues and foreign policy. He has been an outspoken proponent of cutting off money for the war against Iran.

Progressive activists have urged that Mr. Schumer, 75, face a challenge to remaining in the position. Donors and organizations including MoveOn, Indivisible and the Working Families Party plan to back and mobilize members on behalf of Mr. Van Hollen. They are threatening to back primary challenges against any Democratic senator up for re-election in 2028 who does not come out in support of him.

Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont who aligns with Democrats, has said he would oppose Mr. Schumer and encouraged Mr. Van Hollen to become a candidate.

Mr. Schumer and his allies have been adamant that he has more than enough votes to hold the position. But secret ballot leadership votes can be unpredictable. Some senators have refrained from going public with their support to avoid coming under pressure from those urging that Mr. Schumer be deposed.

Mr. Van Hollen says he was not deterred by Mr. Schumer’s claim on the votes to prevail.

“Circumstances change,” he said. “It is one thing to have someone’s support when you’re the only choice. I think a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus is a good thing.”

Lisa Lerer and Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

item.title: After Influence Peddling Claims, White House Restricts Lobbyist Meetings
item.description:
President Trump’s new White House chief of staff is wasting little time trying to differentiate himself from his predecessor.

The office of Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump aide who was elevated to chief of staff last week after Susie Wiles was ousted, issued a memo forbidding White House staff from meeting with lobbyists about policy issues on the building’s grounds without prior approval, according to a person who received the memo and was not authorized to disclose it.

“No President in history has fought more relentlessly, selflessly or courageously for the American People than President Trump,” reads the memo. “Following his example, White House staff are expected to dedicate their time unwaveringly to the working people of the nation.”

The White House did not respond to questions on Thursday night about the memo and what prompted it.

The memo, which was posted on social media by a podcaster allied with Mr. Trump on Thursday and also reported by Politico, follows claims last week by a former top Trump administration health adviser who accused the White House of catering to lobbyists and their clients raising significant funds for the president’s political groups and projects.

Calley Means, a prominent figure in the Make America Healthy Again movement, blamed Ms. Wiles.

Mr. Means, who resigned last month from the Department of Health and Human Services, contended that Ms. Wiles tilted administration health policy to favor corporate donors who hired well-connected lobbyists over ordinary Americans.

He specifically cited Ballard Partners, a lobbying firm where Ms. Wiles once worked, and Ms. Wiles’s daughter, Katie Wiles, who is a partner at the lobbying firm Continental Strategy.

“So if you’re a special interest and you want to get something done, the secret’s out,” Mr. Means said during an interview on The Joe Rogan Experience podcast. “You pay Susie’s daughter, and it was openly discussed when they had a client.”

The White House pushed back on the claims and has said that Katie Wiles did not discuss her business with her mother.

Continental Strategy has said that Katie Wiles does not lobby the U.S. government on behalf of any clients.

Susie Wiles did not respond to requests for comment on Thursday night.

Ballard Partners and its founder, Brian Ballard, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Thursday night.

But in a statement posted on social media on Sunday, Mr. Ballard said his firm’s interactions with Ms. Wiles as chief of staff were “limited and have been the exception, not the rule.”

Mr. Ballard has helped facilitate access to the president and his team for clients who have donated to the Trump-backed super PAC, the White House ballroom project and other projects favored by Mr. Trump. Those clients have sometimes benefited from changes in administration policy.

It is a far cry from 2016, when Mr. Trump ran as a Washington outsider promising to “drain the swamp.”

Mr. Miller started working for Mr. Trump during that campaign.

The podcaster who posted the memo, Benny Johnson, called it “a marked break” from Ms. Wiles’s leadership “and a signal that there is a massive crackdown coming.”

The memo requires Mr. Trump’s staff to receive approval from the White House Counsel’s Office for meetings in the White House complex with registered lobbyists.

Staff are asked to refer lobbyist inquiries to the Office of Public Liaison, the memo instructs, calling the office “the primary point of contact for engagement with external stakeholders.”

The memo nonetheless leaves wiggle room for special interests. Lobbyists could meet staff at venues Mr. Trump frequents outside of the White House complex, like his Mar-a-Lago resort and golf clubs. And many corporate executives have direct relationships with Mr. Trump, independent of their lobbyists.
